entries.title: overclaim — scores an agent's completion claim against a hidden check it never saw and reports the false-completion rate; in its intervention study a verify prompt and both Stop-hook modes gave no detectable reduction
entries.why: Python 3.11+ CLI with no runtime dependencies (v0.1.0) that labels the claim in a coding agent's own final message (complete, partial, incomplete or none) and scores it against an independent hidden check the agent never saw. It reports the false-completion rate (FCR: of the failed runs, how many said "done"), the false-claim share (of the "done" messages, how many were wrong) and what the agent's own tests showed before it claimed success, and it ships a Claude Code Stop hook that sends the agent back once when it claims success with no passing test run after its last edit, or in audit mode asks for a requirement-by-requirement check. Study 1 (Claude Code 2.1.296, Claude Haiku 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 at low and high effort, 18 solvable and 5 impossible Python tasks, 184 trials, $28.88): failed solvable runs were reported as done 11 of 14 times, FCR 78.6% [50.0, 100.0], and 11 of 98 "done" messages were wrong; in 10 of the 11 the agent's last test run after its last edit had passed (the 11th was unreadable). Flagging "done" without a passing test after the last edit caught 1 of 11, with 14 false alarms among the 87 correct "done" messages; an LLM judge also caught 1 of 11. Study 2 (Haiku 5.5, 18 solvable tasks; arms control, ask-verify, stop-hook in claim mode and stop-audit; 288 trials, $28.08): FCR 5/6, 6/9, 5/9 and 6/7, paired differences in false-completion incidence against control +1.4, 0.0 and +1.4 percentage points, all p = 1.00; the claim-mode hook blocked 10 of 72 trials, 9 of which passed, and the audit hook blocked all 72 once. "The study found no support for a Stop hook preventing false completions." Fit: under our code-decides-done rule a deterministic check, not the agent's self-report, decides done (2026-09-25-code-decides-done-and-replay-check), and claimcheck's card is the source of our claim-vs-record check, where a done claim must match the session record; proof-of-done's card blocks a tests-pass claim unless the transcript shows the command ran after the last relevant edit and succeeded, close to this repo's claim mode and to the detector that caught 1 of 11 here. overclaim's rate is a way to test whether such a gate changes anything. Caveats, from its Limitations: one agent family, Python tasks only and few failures (14 failed solvable trials in study 1, 31 in study 2), so the README says to read the rates as rough; 6 of the 11 study-1 false completions come from one task whose hidden check contradicts its prompt (without it, FCR 5/6 and a false-claim share of 5.4%); the labels come from LLMs, all Claude models, and the rule classifier was partly tuned on these messages; in study 2 the hook sat in the workspace's .claude/ directory, where the agent could read it; a failed hidden check counts as ground truth, and hidden checks can be wrong too; every number is the author's run, not ours; MIT, 1 star, created 2026-10-11; README, docs/results.md and docs/hook.md read, not installed or run. Reference only; any live-seat install, hook, or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat, no Herdr. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: cheat-drill — feeds 39 known agent cheat moves to Claude Code PreToolUse hooks and permission rules, scoring cheats blocked next to legit actions blocked; a typical path-based protected-files hook stops 9 of 39
entries.why: Python 3.8+ CLI with no dependencies (v0.1.0) that feeds 39 ways an agent can weaken its own checks to the PreToolUse command hooks and permission rules it collects from user and project settings: sed -i on a test, --no-verify, core.hooksPath, overwriting a golden file, HUSKY=0, assume-unchanged, base64 | sh and more, in seven categories, among them 13 shell routes to the test and verifier files and 9 ways to skip or disable git hooks. It builds a throwaway fixture repo, runs every matching hook for real with the stdin JSON Claude Code sends, approximates the permission matcher, and scores blocked, ask and got through per category, with false blocks on 15 legit controls reported next to the score; nothing in a scenario is ever executed, and --unattended counts ask as got through. The author's measured configs: no guard 0/39; permission deny rules on tests/CI paths plus --no-verify 10/39; a typical path-based protected-files hook 9/39, with 0 of the 13 shell routes; the reference verifier_guard.py 36/39 with 3 ask, an in-sample number because it was written while looking at these scenarios. On 25 held-out cheat variants and 14 controls written afterwards (scripts/heldout.py), v0.1.0 denies 21/25, asks on 1 and lets 3 through (export HUSKY=0; git commit with the variable set in a separate statement, a Python heredoc that writes a test, GIT_CONFIG_PARAMETERS setting core.hooksPath), and wrongly denies 1/14 controls (touch tests/test_new.py). Both path-based setups' one legit block is adding a brand-new test file: "Blanket tests/** rules punish the behaviour you want." Fit: Kanon's card (a guard must be able to fail) and agent-receipts' card (flags || true and commits made with --no-verify, after the fact) are in our playbook as #check-can-fail; cheat-drill is the same kind of probe for a hook guard, known cheat moves in and blocked or not out, with false blocks counted too. tamperproof's card describes a guard with a shell allowlist so sed --in-place, node -e, python -c and redirects don't slip through, which still allows new test files: the two weak spots the drill found in both path-based setups. Caveats: only Claude Code's hook protocol for now (Codex and Gemini CLI formats are on its roadmap), so of our seats in AGENTS.md only Claude Code is covered; non-command hooks are listed as skipped and managed settings are not read; permission-rule results approximate Claude Code's matcher, while hook results are exact because the hooks actually ran; the README says a PreToolUse hook is not a sandbox, since shell parsing can always be outrun, and pairs the guard with a hash check of the verifier in CI; "The drill measures any guard; this one is a starting point, not a solved problem"; every score is the author's run, not ours; MIT, 0 stars, created 2026-10-14; README, scripts/heldout.py and cheat_drill/scenarios.py read, not installed or run. Reference only; any live-seat install, hook, or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat, no Herdr. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: Harness Wrangler — controlled experiments over coding-agent harness patterns: repeated graded runs per task and variant, a confidence interval on the difference, and a baseline with no room to improve reported as no headroom
entries.why: Rust CLI and desktop app (real runs need Claude Code installed and logged in) that measures whether skills, CLAUDE.md files, hooks, system prompt appends, effort levels and models actually help, by how much, and which parts carry the effect. A pattern is testable when four conditions hold: its effect shows inside one session; the result can be checked by a rule, a test command or a rubric judge; the baseline leaves room, because if the agent already gets the task right without the pattern no variant can show a gain (the report calls this "no headroom"; when every task is saturated, that verdict counts as inconclusive, never as "no effect"); and a run is cheap enough to repeat (the default is five runs per cell, and a comparison needs several tasks). Comparisons are paired by task, with 95% hierarchical bootstrap intervals. Graders include test commands, diff size, regex and transcript checks, and a rubric judge whose pairwise comparisons run both orders and count a win only when both agree. wrangler ablate generates leave-one-section-out overlays of a skill or CLAUDE.md to find which sections carry the effect, wrangler trigger-set drafts should-fire and near-miss prompts from a skill's description, a conversation task with a simulated user tests patterns such as asking one question before changing code, and a suite diff on a new model lists patterns that regressed, ones the new model made redundant and ones still earning their keep. For review skills you build the ground truth, fixtures with planted defects and safe-looking decoys, each one verified, and small fixtures saturate: "In one project a plain single pass found every planted defect in fixtures of up to 200 lines, which left a multi-agent review skill nothing to win"; run --baseline-only before paying for the variants. Fit: the three-run-proof-detection-floor card says three runs only catch large regressions and asks for paired comparisons with error bars; agent-evals' card became our replay regression check inside Three-Run Proof, where a replay pass means nothing broke, not that the change is good (2026-09-25-code-decides-done-and-replay-check); recalibrate-or-retire's card asks, when a model in the path changes, whether each rule still earns its place, the question the suite diff answers per pattern. Caveats: no LICENSE file, and GitHub reports no license (the Cargo workspace manifest declares MIT, but no license text ships), so it is pattern only: read and re-implement the idea; copy no file and vendor no code. By its own list, poor fits are skills whose payoff spans sessions (memory, notes), skills that act outside the workspace, and permission and safety behaviour, since runs use bypassPermissions; the 200-line finding is one project's experience; 0 stars, created 2026-10-13; README and Cargo.toml read, not built or run. Any real experiment is model spend and a separate Haiyuan decision. Reference only; any live-seat install, hook, or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat, no Herdr. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: agent-perch — one-file stdlib Python supervisor for always-on agents in tmux: frozen means an unchanged screen and a known marker, a known dialog gets its keys instead of a restart, a usage-limit banner only alerts
entries.why: Single-file supervisor (perch.py: Python 3.11+, standard library only, needs tmux), extracted from the watchdog a fleet of always-on Claude Code agents needed on a Raspberry Pi. A one-shot tick run from cron reads agents.toml (cmd, cwd, auto_replies, restart_markers, notice_regex and an optional health_cmd), restarts a dead session, and halts an agent with one alert after 3 restarts in 10 minutes. Its design rules: frozen = unchanged screen AND a known marker, because "Either signal alone misfires: an idle agent at a prompt has an unchanged screen; a working agent shows a marker-like word mid-output"; markers match the last 10 lines after trailing whitespace is removed; interior blank lines count, idle_markers veto stuck_markers, and restart_markers restart at once for prompts nothing can answer, such as arrow-key menus; auto_replies answer a known harness dialog with keys from your config, since a restart would just show it again; notice_regex observes and never acts, so a usage-limit banner is alert only, suppressing consecutive repeats of the same last matching line; a reappearing banner can alert again; health_cmd restarts after 2 consecutive failures, for a hung agent whose screen looks normal (the fleet needed a check that its MCP child process was alive); and the mailbox is a file, not keystroke injection ("Typing into another agent's terminal corrupts whatever it is mid-way through"): a jsonl append under flock with per-reader cursors, so agents must poll, plus an opt-in doorbell that types one fixed line telling an idle agent to read it. Alerts go through your own notify_cmd, with credentials kept out of the config, and the dashboard binds 127.0.0.1 and is read-only unless PERCH_TOKEN is set (a Tailscale login named in PERCH_TS_USER can also skip the token). Fit: grok-tmux-watchdog acts on a stale log (~540s) and resumes the same session (2026-09-05-stream-json-watchdog-all-runs); juli-os/agents' pane probes tell awaiting input from still working, and tmux-agent-status reads a status the agent writes itself; perch adds rules for when a screen should and should not cause a restart. A perch restart is tmux kill-session followed by a new session, with no check that the old process exited; our watchdog resume-safety rule resumes a stale run only after the old process is confirmed gone, and until its code goes live the EM checks by hand (confirm-old-process-dead-before-resume's card). Caveats, its own: markers are per-agent config you must know up front, and the strings must be adjusted to your Claude Code version; "liveness is 'session exists', not 'work is progressing'"; alerts have no delivery guarantee or retry; single machine, single tenant, no per-agent CPU or memory limits, and no auth, secrets management or isolation between agents, which share a Unix user; the resource check reads /proc/meminfo, with a Pi's default thresholds; MIT, 0 stars, created 2026-10-05; README, perch.py and docs/case-study.md read, not installed or run. Reference only; any live-seat install, hook, or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat, no Herdr. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: Agentic Vault Skeleton — Obsidian vault template: one AGENTS.md that CLAUDE.md only imports, a three-file map marking what is off limits, a skill catalog read instead of the skills, a cache of the last two sessions
entries.why: Obsidian vault template, part of the author's Digital Brain repos, laid out so that any AI agent can find its way around without reading everything. Its rules: "I write; agents read and enrich": your notes are yours, and agents link them and summarize sources next to them, but never rewrite them. One rules file for every agent: AGENTS.md holds the working rules and CLAUDE.md only imports it (@AGENTS.md), so Claude Code, Codex, Hermes or any other runtime follow the same rules. A map, not a scan: three small files in 0 - System/, me.md (who you are), vault-map.md (each folder's contents and permission; the private folder is off limits, with no read, write, list, index or memory, and every scan starts at a content folder, never at the vault root) and skills-index.md (name, trigger, role). Lazy-loaded skills: "The agent reads the skill catalog, not the skills"; a skill's full instructions load only when a request matches its trigger, and a new capability is one skill folder plus one row. Memory between sessions: the agent reads _cache.md at session start and adds a dated block at the end, then trim_cache.py keeps the 2 most recent sessions and moves older ones to _cache-archive.md, backing both files up first. Privacy is a folder, enforced by a separate repo, vault-privacy-guard, which the README lists as a pre-tool hook that keeps every agent out of the private folder. Fit: our vault AGENTS.md applies to every agent, and install-agent-hooks.sh wires it into the agy, Codex, Kimi and DSH homes and the home and project roots, copies a global CLAUDE.md and installs the shared skills into the DSH, Muse and .agents skill homes (2026-09-15-muse-dsh-vault-skills-hooks). ai-baton's card has the same one-rules-file shape (WORKSPACE.md loaded by every session through a CLAUDE.md import on a clone); the memory loop card's recall step scans the one-line summaries and loads only the files that apply, as the skill catalog does for skills; and agent-docs-lint's unreferenced_agent check asks whether any doc names an agent or skill file, the drift a hand-kept catalog can develop. Caveats: hooks.json is written in plain language, so the session-start read and the session-end write and trim are instructions the agent follows because AGENTS.md says so, not hooks a runtime executes; the privacy guard lives in that separate repo, not fetched here; it is a starter layout (me.md is a template, skills-index.md holds one example row); MIT, 0 stars, created 2026-10-13; README, AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, the 0 - System/ files and trim_cache.py read, not installed or run. Reference only; any live-seat install, hook, or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat, no Herdr. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: CyrilXBT (@cyrilXBT) — memory loop: write only what is new, one-line summaries first, consolidation deletes, say what recall applied
entries.why: CyrilXBT's article (dated Jul 11, 2026 on the threadnavigator mirror) argues that memory is compression, not a longer transcript, and builds it in four steps. Write: after a session, record only what is not already in the code, the chat history or an existing note, one lesson per file with a one-line summary on top. Consolidate: on a schedule, merge duplicate lessons and delete the ones that turned out wrong or outdated: 'deleted entirely, not archived, deleted'. Recall: at the start, scan the summaries, load only the files that apply, and say so when nothing does. Apply: at the end, name the recalled lesson that changed the work, or confirm none did; a lesson that keeps going unused means its summary or the search needs fixing. Fit: the vault and each agent's own memory get the same loop inside the existing daily consolidation, with no new routine; the post-task note template gains a summary line, a 'New?' line and a 'Recalled lessons applied' line, and the done receipt gains that last line. Caveats: our standing rule allows deletions only after Haiyuan's explicit approval of the specific items, so consolidation merges duplicates directly but puts wrong or outdated lessons, an agent's private memory included, on a named prune list; approved items are deleted, not archived, and Decision notes are preserved; the article is written around one model but says the protocol is not built-in model behavior, so every model in the path must be told it; its prompts, weekly cadence, monthly audit and per-project folders are the author's process, not measured here, and only the four rules were taken. In playbook (2026-10-13, Haiyuan-approved) §4: https://caohy1988.github.io/research/harness/#memory-loop.
keeps: write only what is new: check the code, the chat or PR thread and existing notes first; update or cite instead of restating
one-line summary on top of every new note; recall scans the summaries first and opens only the notes that apply

consolidation merges duplicates directly; wrong or outdated lessons, private memory included, go on a named prune list, and only items Haiyuan approves are deleted, not archived (direct deletion only for agent-owned scratch; Decision notes preserved)
say 'nothing applies' at recall; the post-task note and done receipt name the recalled lesson that changed the work, or 'none applied'
skippedAsCovered: per-project memory folders (covered: five buckets + shared-memory admission rule)
weekly consolidation cadence (folded into the existing daily consolidation; no new routine)
monthly memory-value audit (not adopted: a new standing cost)
verify a lesson before writing it (covered: claim vs record, code decides done)
tell a newly switched model the protocol (covered: AGENTS.md is wired into every CLI home by install-agent-hooks.sh)

entries.title: workflow-script-harness — test harness that runs a Claude Code Workflow-tool script unmodified under node:test, with scripted per-label agent responses, a counter trace for proving overlap and named sandbox errors
entries.why: Node test harness (Node 18+; the whole implementation is one file, src/harness.js, with zero runtime dependencies) for scripts written against Claude Code's Dynamic Workflows feature, the Workflow tool's DSL (agent(), pipeline(), parallel(), phase(), log(), args, budget). It reproduces that sandbox in Node's built-in vm module, so a script runs unmodified under node:test with no real Claude Code session, no real agents and no network. agentResponses scripts agent() per label, in call order: { type: 'null' } resolves to null to simulate a failed or empty agent call, and a label whose responses run out raises a clear error. budget takes a total and an ordered spentSequence that each budget.spent() call consumes, so budget-aware branches are testable too. parallel() runs its tasks concurrently with Promise.all, and pipeline() lets independent items overlap across stages while a given item's stage 2 never starts before its own stage 1 finished; result.trace records monotonic counters, not timestamps, so a test checks overlap with a.startCounter < b.endCounter && b.startCounter < a.endCounter, with no wall-clock flakiness. Date, Math, require, process and other host or non-deterministic primitives are blocked with a named FORBIDDEN_PRIMITIVE error when called or when their properties are read, and calling an unknown global or reading its properties throws UNKNOWN_GLOBAL; in both cases, capturing an untouched reference inside a returned object can succeed. A HarnessError (a test or config problem: fix the test) is always distinguishable by .name from a ScriptError (the script's own bug, such as a TypeError: fix the script). Fit: harness-mocks' claude-mock stands in for the claude binary and agent-evals records model calls once and replays them offline; this stands in for the agents a Workflow-tool script calls. Its FAQ still asks for a final real run before a script is trusted in production, close to how our replay regression check sits inside Three-Run Proof, where live Three-Run Proof stays the bar (2026-09-25-code-decides-done-and-replay-check). Caveats: the sandbox semantics are a point-in-time snapshot that the README dates as last verified against the Workflow tool on 2026-09-09; allowed globals or concurrency behaviour can change at any time, and the README asks for an issue naming your Claude Code version if they drift; the harness is not a security boundary (Node's vm is not hardened against a malicious script), which the README says is fine because the script under test is yours; it targets Claude Code's Workflow tool, so it applies only where a Claude Code seat runs such scripts; the author built it to test their own Workflow-tool scripts, with no formal support commitment; npm package, MIT, 0 stars, created 2026-09-09; README-verified, not installed or run. Reference only; any live-seat install, hook, or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat, no Herdr. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: The Docket — Claude Code plugin: a ledger of numbered rulings, a pre-edit hook that prints the rulings cited within twenty lines, and a judge at the stop that can block it on a FAIL or STALE verdict
entries.why: Claude Code plugin (v0.1.0; needs Node 20+, git and the claude CLI) that keeps a repository's decisions from being undone, built around a ledger the agent doing the work (the README's maker) cannot walk past. A ledger is a Markdown file of numbered rulings (docs/DECISIONS.md, or your own), each with the principle it was resolved against, its reason and what it does to earlier rulings, an edge named by one of a fixed list of verbs: a later ruling supersedes an earlier one, often a single clause of it, and never edits it away. Before an edit, a hook prints the rulings cited within twenty lines of it, nearest first, with the edges among them; it informs and never blocks. At the stop, if the session's diff touches a governed file (one that cites a ruling), a ledger or a spec beside one, the hook starts a judge: a headless session of its own, allowed to read files and run the docket's core, which records its verdict. The judge scores the diff against the rulings and its domain packs, and a FAIL, or a STALE for a ruling whose reason the diff has made untrue, blocks the stop with located failures: FAIL directs the maker to change the code or supersede the ruling through /rule; STALE directs it to a dated addendum through /rule. /rule asks five questions, refuses a vague answer and writes nothing until you type confirm in a turn of your own. The witness that checks the rulings is a node script your repository owns and your CI runs, so they still govern after the plugin is uninstalled. Measured results are dated ledger records; the latest judge record (2026-10-02, Claude Code 2.1.287) printed "every outcome: met" over six scenarios, each judge ending 23 to 35 seconds after it started. Fit: our standing rules are dated Maps/Decisions/ locks behind one-line AGENTS.md pointers, and a later lock can narrow part of an earlier one (AGENTS.md's Jev pre-launch step cites 2026-09-24-jev-fleet-shadow-token-gate with § Q8 of 2026-09-27-lab-keeps-folded-into-playbook); the Docket keeps that shape inside a code repository and adds a judge of the diff. wordcell's card calls its path-scoped context the missing retrieval bridge between our Decisions/forbidden.md and the file under edit, the job the Docket's pre-edit hook does for a repository's own rulings. Caveats, from its Known Limits: the maker's session may run the core and record a verdict, so the boundary is permission and visibility, not cryptography; the judge is a model reading prose that most likely shares the maker's model and its blind spots; the stale reading is the weakest, met in 1 of 2 further runs; each governed stop costs a headless session on your account, with at most 5 judged blocks per session between passes and the judge bounded at 700 seconds; every measurement ran on one host, and no measurement of the hook has had a control; 0 stars, created 2026-09-11, MIT; README-verified, not installed or run. Reference only; any live-seat install, hook, or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat, no Herdr. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: prove-it-done — agent skill for receipt-gated completion: one-line receipts a bundled verifier re-runs, self-reports recorded but never counted, and two confirmations through one instrument counted as one
entries.why: Agent skill (SKILL.md plus scripts/verify_receipts.py, which needs Python 3.9 or later and nothing else) that puts a small, mechanical step between the work and the word done. A receipt is a one-line check, written in a Markdown ledger, that the bundled verifier re-runs against the real system and judges PASS or FAIL. Receipt kinds: cmd: (no shell), sh: (shell, off unless --allow-shell is given), file: (exists, SHA-256), dir:, http: (status, body text), commit: (exists, touches a path, on a branch) and said: (a recorded self-report, never counted). Six rules: a self-report is a claim, not evidence; a confirmation names its instrument, and two through the same instrument count as one; a config check is not a behaviour check; a check that errors proves nothing; a check must come after the last change; reopen, never delete, so a done step whose receipt fails is reopened with strike-through, not deleted. In the README's example, run with --min-instruments 2, a deploy tool's "ok: rollout started" prints as CLAIM and does not count, while an http: receipt and a cmd: receipt through kubectl pass, so the step is PROVEN through 2 instruments. Install is a copy into the skills folder of Claude Code or any runtime that loads SKILL.md skills. Fit: our done receipt's VERIFIED lists only checks that ran, with evidence (2026-09-27-0xjmori-harness-receipt-and-disproof-review), and under code decides done a deterministic check (tests, file, commit or live URL) beats an agent self-report (2026-09-25-code-decides-done-and-replay-check); cmd:, file:, commit: and http: receipts cover similar ground as one-liners, and the instrument rule would add a count of independent sources to a VERIFIED line. proof-of-done blocks a tests-pass, build or deploy claim at the stop unless the transcript shows the command ran after the last relevant edit and succeeded, and gatehouse binds evidence to GATES.md oracles; this is a skill the agent follows, not a hook. Caveats, from its Limits: it is a skill, not a gate, so nothing stops an agent from skipping it unless the verifier's exit status is wired into a hook or CI step; the verifier checks receipts, not whether they are the right receipts, and via= and proves=config are labels the agent applies honestly or not; instrument names are guessed from the receipt (program name, HTTP host), so two tools reading the same source look independent unless tagged with the same via=; http: sends no credentials; no effect size is claimed, since the eval harness has been tested on four synthetic transcripts only; 0 stars, created 2026-10-11, MIT; README-verified, not installed or run. Reference only; any live-seat install, hook, or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat, no Herdr. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: bouncer — Claude Code PreToolUse judgment layer: hard rules and a fast path decide in code before any model call, seven Jev questions judge the middle against a YAML policy, and it ships in observe mode
entries.why: Claude Code plugin (Node 20+, zero runtime dependencies) whose PreToolUse hook asks TypeSafe Jev, a fast judgment model rather than a frontier LLM, seven plain-English questions about a proposed tool call in one call, for about four cents a day per the README; each answer is a probability, and thresholds in a YAML policy you own act on it. Its stated rule is that the edges are code and the judge decides the middle: gate.hard_rules and the gate.fast_path allowlist decide the cases that should never have been a probability before any model is called. The README's evidence: calibration run 7 cleared the bar on all seven questions, yet the question naming the risk scored cat .env at 0.15; in run 8 a correct friction fix removed the coverage a neighbouring question had given a live Stripe key exported on the command line, which fell through to allow, and the second pass, with hard rules in place, caught it. Modes: observe, the default, emits no decision and logs what it would have said ("a classifier you have not personally watched be wrong is not one to hand a veto to"); seatbelt, for --dangerously-skip-permissions sessions, stays silent until a hard rule matches unless you enable a deny threshold yourself, and a deny under that flag was confirmed by a sentinel probe on 2026-09-18; guard and full are for prompted users. bouncer calibrate runs the policy over labelled near-miss pairs and prints a pass/fail row per question against 0.85 accuracy at confidence 0.8 or higher; calibrate --gate produces a six-part candidate/reference report covering accuracy, calibration, polarity, rephrase, injection and latency. Latency is not measured, reversed and rephrased variants are skipped until stamped, and no backend can pass or receive an attestation yet; polarity or injection failures disqualify. Fit: company-in-a-box's card records that our Jev layer already had a guard (pre_tool) gate (2026-09-20-jev-decision-layer); gates such as worth_running run in shadow and never block (2026-09-24-jev-fleet-shadow-token-gate), as observe mode does; and our Jev constant baseline asks a gate to beat the always-majority constant before shadow→active (2026-09-27-lab-keeps-folded-into-playbook; archestra's card), a different bar from calibrate's accuracy row. Caveats: its 112 hand-labelled fixtures measure agreement with one person's policy intuitions, not ground truth; it catches mistakes and is not a security boundary; a judged call sends Jev a state (the tool, the command, what its paths mean), and the jev backend reads BOUNCER_TYPESAFE_API_KEY, while jev-belay's card notes our router reaches Jev through OpenRouter; the README gives both nineteen and twenty-two hard rules, so no count is quoted here; 1 star, created 2026-09-18, MIT; README-verified, not installed or run. Any live gating or model-call spend is a separate Haiyuan decision. Reference only; any live-seat install, hook, or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat, no Herdr. entries.title: five-second-report — Claude Code and Codex Stop hook that asks for a re-send, by default, at most twice a session, when a change-making turn's final message lacks status sections or has a detected structural violation
entries.why: Stop hook for Claude Code and OpenAI Codex (Node 18+, one hooks/report.js file; the README says no dependencies) for running many agents at once, when each turn ends in a wall of prose and you cannot tell which agent is finished, which is stuck and which is waiting on you. When a turn ends, the hook reads the session transcript: a turn that only read things or chatted stays silent, and a turn that changed something should end in up to seven sections, in order, empty ones left out: BROKEN, IN PROGRESS, DONE, DISPATCHED, QUEUED, PENDING, DECISION, with ALL FINISHED when nothing is left open; a PENDING item says what you must do (the README's example: "you: run the deploy script; I have no access to the prod server."). A detected change-making turn without status sections triggers a re-send. Certain structural violations also trigger one, including out-of-order sections and excessive item counts. Missing bold titles can pass unnoticed; preamble, trailing-text and soft-ask warnings accompany another violation rather than independently triggering a re-send. A DECISION section without an AskUserQuestion call in the recognized turn triggers a picker request. It answers with a block decision that does not reject the turn: the agent re-sends the message fixed, so you never see the bad version. It ignores re-sends it triggered itself, remembers each message it already complained about, defaults to firing at most twice per session, configurable through STATUS_FORMAT_MAX_FIRES, and CLAUDE_DISABLE_STATUS_FORMAT=1 turns it off. The hook only enforces the format, so the agent must be told it first: the FORMAT.md text goes in CLAUDE.md or an output style, or AGENTS.md for Codex. Its tests feed it fake Claude Code and Codex transcripts. Fit: Gate Inbox reads the tmux panes to show sessions blocked on you, tmux-agent-status reads each agent's own session state, and overnight-receipts lists what an agent's final message left undone or asked; this puts the who-owes-next answer in the final message itself. Our done receipt (OBJECTIVE / CHANGED / VERIFIED / NOT VERIFIED / RISKS / APPROVAL NEEDED) covers Github PR/job and Manage non-trivial done reports, not each turn (2026-09-27-0xjmori-harness-receipt-and-disproof-review), and oversight-readable-output's trial asks for short controlled-language reports Haiyuan must judge; a DONE section here is shape, not evidence. Caveats: of our seats in AGENTS.md, only Claude Code and Codex are covered; Codex skips an untrusted hook with no warning until it is trusted in /hooks; Context Guard's card notes our fleet runs are mostly one-shot grok-tmux-run jobs, not long interactive chats; 0 stars, created 2026-10-12, MIT; README-verified, not installed or run. entries.title: overnight-receipts — zero-dependency CLI reads Claude Code session JSONL plus git branches and prints a per-branch receipt ranked worst-first with a merge/fix/kill suggestion and a needs-you list
entries.why: Zero-dependency triage CLI (Node ≥ 22 and git, nothing to build) for the morning after unattended Claude Code runs: it parses the session logs already on disk under ~/.claude/projects and the local git branches, then prints one receipt per branch. A receipt carries a status (FAILED, UNVERIFIED or PASSED, taken from the last test or lint command — a test piped into tail that exits 0 is never PASSED), a merge/fix/kill suggestion with its reason (it never suggests merge without a passing test run), the task's first prompt, the session id and transcript path with a line reference per field, the last test command and its exit code, commit diff stats, retry counts, risk labels (dependency, data, auth, payments), out-of-area files, and a "needs you" list of what the agent's final message left undone or asked. Ranking is worst-first; a digest subcommand writes one file across repos atomically, and --json has a published schema. The repo is a 2026-10-11 rename of dawnlog, the npm name belonging to an unrelated tool. Safety: without --summarize the only subprocess is git and nothing touches the network (a test traps subprocesses and sockets to assert it), and all output is secret-redacted across 12 formats, best-effort; --summarize is the one option that runs anything else, your own claude -p, redacted first. Fit: our Mac CLIs run unattended overnight through grok-tmux-run, and the done-receipt rule (2026-09-27-0xjmori-harness-receipt-and-disproof-review) wants VERIFIED backed by checks that ran; a receipt built from test exit codes and git state is that evidence, next to titan-receipts (receipts checked in CI using a pinned verifier rather than the copy in the audited repo), receipt-pr-agent-cost-ledger and completion-check-evidence-not-narrative. Caveats: it assumes the Claude Code project JSONL layout and matches sessions to branches by branch name, worktree or commit times, so runs whose branches do not line up land under Unmatched; redaction is best-effort — a token format not on the list leaks; 228 node:test tests; 0 stars, created 2026-10-11, MIT; README-verified, not installed or run. entries.title: agent-chain-doctor — one read-only shell script audits a scheduled agent chain (launchd / cron / systemd + the session script) against 30 silent-stop checks, verdict exposed, guarded or undecidable with the evidence printed
entries.why: A single shell script — no dependencies, no network, no writes, no privileges, running on the stock macOS bash 3.2 — that inspects the chain a scheduled agent runs through (launchd, cron or systemd plus the session script they launch) and returns, for each of 30 checks, exposed, guarded or undecidable (UNKNOWN in the report: a check that measured nothing is UNKNOWN, never GUARDED, and evidence prints under every EXPOSED). Exit 0 means nothing exposed, 1 something exposed, 2 the tool refused to diagnose. The failure shapes come from the author's own chain: a wakeup trigger file emptied by a failing date, a stale lock nothing clears, traps covering EXIT only, a scheduler PATH missing the agent's own binary, a laptop asleep through the window. Extras include extras/startup-watchdog, which kills a run that has printed nothing after N seconds instead of waiting out a multi-hour timeout, plus an MCP server (Python 3 stdlib, stdio, read-only) exposing the same 30 checks as diagnose_scheduled_agent. The honesty contract is stated up front: zero EXPOSED means "these 30 checks found nothing", never "your chain is fine" — the false-negative rate is unknown and, the README says, will stay unknown — and the suite is mutation-tested (30 checks × 2 mutants), with a published account of its own GUARDED line having been wrong twice. Fit: a job that never starts produces no job output, while a local scheduler may leave diagnostic traces; our launch standard pairs stream-json with grok-tmux-watchdog on a ~540s stale log (2026-09-05-stream-json-watchdog-all-runs) and vigil's card reports a window nothing tried as missed from outside, while this audits the launch chain before the window, beside loop-orchestrator-tmux-watchdog, confirm-old-process-dead-before-resume and the 2026-09-15-field-brief-miss-watch second line. Caveats: it is not a liveness monitor and cannot tell whether the agent did good work; hosted schedulers are unreadable from the machine, and its missed-run-check only tells you the same hour it skipped; the checks are heuristic; 12 open issues; 0 stars, created 2026-09-13, MIT; README-verified, not installed or run. entries.title: starlane — stdlib-only Python harness around a Markdown vault: mapcheck link and secret audit, read-only specialist agents behind an Atlas dispatcher, scheduled routines with time limit, daily cap and circuit breaker
entries.why: A personal tool made public — the README's own honest note says not a framework and not production software, shared as is — that runs a small harness over an Obsidian-style vault plus the Claude Code CLI, in four layers, stdlib-only Python 3.11+: Memory (aos mapcheck checks broken links, a two-hop navigation rule, frontmatter and leaked secrets), Agent (a roster of specialist agents whose tools come from a fixed whitelist — vault Read, Grep, Glob, with WebSearch and WebFetch only for an agent declared mixed, which is then told never to put note text into a search or URL — routed by an Atlas dispatcher; agents can read, they cannot write, run commands or push), Pulse (aos tick runs whitelisted routines without a shell, each with a time limit, a daily cap and a circuit breaker, the risky ones off by default), and Screen (aos serve, a local 127.0.0.1 dashboard behind a per-start token showing vault health, routine timelines, agent status and spend). entries.title: dsh-doc-review — DSH plugin: a per-session activated doc_review tool spawns an isolated sub-agent review with a JSON Schema report, a pre-spawn token cost gate and multi-round convergence tracking
entries.why: DeepSeek Harness plugin (Node.js ≥ 20, host @deepseek-ai/dsh >=0.2.0-rc.1 <0.3.0) that keeps document reviews out of the main session. Since v0.2.0 the doc_review tool is not globally resident: a session must run the /doc-review slash command first, which registers the tool in that session's scope only — idempotent, revoked when the session closes, and a session that never activated gets no schema at all. On a call it spawns an isolated sub-agent session with no external tools by default (web_search and web_fetch only under web_fact_check: true) and reviews the document against four toggleable dimensions — fact, completeness, necessity, format — returning a JSON Schema-constrained report (each issue carries id, dimension, severity, a location containing either a verbatim quote of at least 8 consecutive document characters or a Markdown heading line, claim, evidence and suggestion), an adjudication template and a next_action. A conservative token estimate runs before any spawn: a worst case over 20,000 tokens returns confirmationRequired without spawning, a chain-cumulative projection over 20,000 × max_rounds is blocked again, and one confirmation holds per chain_id. Multi-round chains (default 1 round, hard cap 3) read the archived previous round back, compute a line- and character-level LCS change ratio, align issues across rounds (an unmatched old issue counts as resolved, an unmatched new one as added — the plugin recounts, not the reviewer) and stop on convergence (change ratio under 3.0%, or no high-severity issue and zero recomputed new ones, or the cap). Each round archives document.md, review-report.json and change-log.md under .doc-review/<chain_id>/, with chain-cost.json at the root; tests run under node --test with zero LLM calls and zero network. Fit: our locked doc workflow (2026-09-28-opus-draft-astra-fable-review, 2026-10-06-reviewer-rule-docs-vs-code) runs blind reviews whose commentary should not bloat the drafting session; an isolated sub-agent with a schema-locked report is that shape for the DSH seat, beside portable-dsh-multi-agent-plugin and dsh-cos-verify-handoffs, and the pre-spawn cost gate is the run-limits rule (2026-09-23-0xjmori-run-limits-ladder-retry) inside the tool. Caveats: the README is in Chinese; it depends on the host's subagents spawn provider and degrades to same-session without it; references never fetch URLs; it is built against 0.2.0 preview hosts whose kernel API may change before a stable release; 0 stars, created 2026-10-12, MIT; README-verified, not installed or run. entries.title: clear-resume — Claude Code plugin that saves a plain-text handover (goal, next action, status, decisions, failed attempts) into ~/.clear-resume before /clear or cache expiry and loads it in the fresh session
entries.why: Claude Code plugin (Node ≥ 18 and git; one skill, three hooks, one mod) for pausing a long chat without losing the task. /clear-resume:handover writes a short plain-text handover into ~/.clear-resume — the goal, the next action, where things stand, the decisions made and what already failed — a file you can open, edit, paste into another chat or load on a second machine; after /clear the fresh session loads it automatically. Two opt-ins sit on top: an idle handover (off by default) that acts about 5 minutes before the prompt cache expires, either as a toast or as auto, which has the handover written while the cache is still warm, clears the session and then waits — it does not keep working while you are away; and a relay mod that runs /clear after each save and continues from the handover, stopping when its clears are used up or two continued sessions in a row make no new commit. The README reports these separate measurements: coming back to a 390k-token session after the 60-minute cache expired cost US$1.56 in each of 3 runs, while a warm handover plus a fresh session reading it cost US$0.15–0.17 in total (n=3, both on Sonnet 5.5, 10 Oct 2026), about 9–10× less — with the caveat that the saving exists only if you come back; moving a 390k-token session to Opus cost US$3.13 against US$0.24 via a scripted handover (n=1); and on a 30-item build the relay and native auto-compaction each finished 5 of 6 runs, with the five completed runs in each group averaging 37.4M vs 35.3M tokens. A handover is under 1% of what /clear removes (about 780 vs 102,088 tokens, medians across the author's 104 clears). Fit: our handoff packet v1 (Maps/Contracts/manage-handoffs.md, 2026-09-25-rari-handoff-packet-repro-first-promotion-gate) similarly preserves the objective and decisions, with the note itself kept on disk where another machine can audit it; it sits next to context-guard-token-ceiling-handoff-checkpoints (forces a handoff note past a ceiling) and claude-code-cache-keepalive (cache collapse visible in the transcript), and compaction-stress-lab's card is the measured account of what a summary loses. Caveats: macOS has not been tested by hand — the author daily-drives Windows 11, a Linux clean install was tested by hand, and CI covers all three; the cost figures are the author's own small-n measurements; the cache-expiry timing is an estimate; handovers are local plain text, so keep secrets out of them; 1 star, created 2026-09-19, MIT; README-verified, not installed or run. entries.title: agent-docs-lint — zero-LLM CLI that flags missing file and slash-command targets, listed model or plan names, unreferenced agent or skill files and broken anchors in agent docs
entries.why: Zero-LLM Python CLI that catches drift in agent documentation, designed for AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, .cursor/rules, .claude/agents, .claude/skills, .agents/skills and similar repos where docs are the source of truth. Four checks: dead_ref (local Markdown links, backtick path-like references or slash commands that point to missing files or command targets), model_name (hard-coded model or plan tokens from a configurable list), unreferenced_agent (agent or skill Markdown files not mentioned by filename stem) and broken_anchor (a local Markdown link whose #anchor is missing in the target file). Exit 0 means no error findings or --warn-only was used, 1 one or more error findings, 2 a CLI, config or runtime error. entries.title: learn-from-mistakes — an agent labels what went wrong; the lfm CLI counts repeated causes per source, never adding sources together, and flags recommendations citing missing records
entries.why: Node CLI (lfm) plus a bundled agent skill for finding the mistakes coding agents keep repeating in records a fleet already writes, such as a defect log or a pipeline's failed steps. The work is split: your agent reads each record and judges what happened, following the skill, and writes the labels and proposed changes; the CLI does the arithmetic: it merges duplicates, counts each source separately, checks that every recommendation cites real records and lists what was never read. The README's example config pairs a Markdown log (each "- " bullet a record, dated by its ## heading) with a no-mistakes store whose failed steps are opened read-only, gives a cause an optional match that counts typed store rows, and sets repeat to min_incidents 3, min_days 2. Log and store counts are shown side by side and never added, a recommendation citing a record that does not exist is named as a problem, and records nobody labelled are reported as unlabelled, never guessed. Exit 0 ok, 1 a label or proposal has a problem, 2 bad usage or config, 3 the sources hold nothing. It never edits sources, instructions or config, makes no network or model calls, and does not apply the recommended changes or measure whether they worked. Fit: our repeat lesson → proposed skill diff rule drafts a fix instead of another forbidden.md paragraph when the correction is already there twice or more (2026-09-27-lab-keeps-folded-into-playbook); lfm adds a spread across days to the count, keeps sources apart and checks that each proposal's evidence resolves. harness-creator mines session history and writes the rules, hooks or skills you approve; lfm only recommends, and its label-then-count step is the one failure-taxonomy's card proposes for our forbidden.md corrections. Caveats: no LICENSE file (GitHub reports none), so treat it as all rights reserved and as pattern only: read and re-implement the idea; copy no file and vendor no code; the README's examples are synthetic (a 13-record defect log, a small no-mistakes store, labels written by following the skill), and its end-to-end tests run the real CLI on synthetic fixtures; needs Node 22.13+; 0 stars, created 2026-10-11; README-verified, not installed or run. entries.title: compaction-stress-lab — 628 runs on two small models: one compaction kept about 1 in 5 exact tool-printed details on real sessions, and a keep-exact paragraph roughly doubled that
entries.why: Study of what native context compaction in the Anthropic and OpenAI APIs makes coding agents forget, measured at the API layer with two small models, Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna: 628 runs across a controlled lab session with 29 facts hidden at known spots (108), 12 recorded SWE-agent sessions (240) and its own API agent fixing 10 SWE-bench Verified bugs in Docker (280). Findings: one compaction keeps about 1 in 5 exact details the tools printed on real sessions (19–20%, against 99–100% with full history); losses compound (GPT-6 Luna 67% → 48% → 30% → 23% over four compactions); summaries keep what was discussed, not what was printed (facts the agent stated 79–91%, facts only in tool output 24–31%); one paragraph of keep-exact instructions, printed in the README, roughly doubled exact recall on real sessions (to 41–48%), though in the live layer it cut steps, not failures; 90–97% of lost values were answered UNKNOWN, yet 7 of 72 rollout plans written after compaction used an outdated value (old DB port, revoked secret, broken release), against 0 of 36 without compaction. Its advice: compact late and rarely, at a task boundary after the agent has stated its results, write exact values to a notes file first, and re-check the source of truth before deploys, rollbacks or secrets. Fit: Context Guard's card notes our fleet runs are mostly one-shot grok-tmux-run jobs, not long interactive chats, so this bears on a seat only where its runs actually compact; there, the notes-file advice sits next to Context Guard's handoff checkpoints and our handoff packet v1, whose artifacts and decisions fields carry paths and decisions already made (2026-09-25-rari-handoff-packet-repro-first-promotion-gate). Caveats: two small models, and the README says larger models compact better (gpt-6.1-sol with instructions kept about 99% in an earlier 10-model run); measured through its own API adapters and agent loop, not inside a coding CLI; live bugs were short (7–15 steps), so compaction was forced early; an AI drafted the real-session questions and code verified them, and the question writer and judge are OpenAI models; code and docs MIT, while inputs/ keep their sources' licenses (CC-BY-4.0 for the recorded sessions); 0 stars, created 2026-10-10; README-verified, not installed or run. entries.title: @juli-os/agents — tmux session runtime: a swallowed Enter is re-sent, never the text; tmux is resolved despite a gutted PATH; pane probes tell awaiting input from still working
entries.why: Bottom layer of the juli-os ladder: a tmux-based agent session runtime in TypeScript with zero npm dependencies (Node built-ins only, Node ≥ 22.5). Its tmux client confirms delivery: sendTextConfirmed polls for the input box to reset, and a swallowed Enter is re-sent, never the text. A startup-time binary resolver survives GUI-launched processes with a gutted PATH (the homebrew ENOENT class of failure), and a side-effect-free CLI inspector (juli-agents bin) prints which tmux binary it resolved. Provisioning dispatch creates or reuses a session, cold-starts claude, and uses pane probes to tell "awaiting input" from "still working". Self-healing is a snapshot/recover loop, zombie fingerprints and a context gate that auto-compacts on a threshold with a cooldown. It also installs Claude Code Stop, SessionStart and PermissionRequest hooks from a spec so agent events flow back to your service, keeps a markdown skill registry, prefers an ACP executor (protocol-level completion) over tmux async when present, and carries orchestrator and voice-call scaffolding with a staged-plan (discuss → proposed → confirmed) call flow. Fit: our long Mac CLI runs launch through grok-tmux-run in tmux, and grok-tmux-watchdog acts on a stale log (~540s) (2026-09-05-stream-json-watchdog-all-runs); a pane read that tells awaiting input from still working would be a second signal there, as tmux-agent-status's card says of a status the agent writes itself, and Gate Inbox also reads the panes, to show sessions blocked on you. agent-quota-tracker's verified poke re-queries the provider rather than trust the poke alone; sendTextConfirmed checks delivery at the input box and retries only the keystroke. Context Guard forces a handoff note past a ceiling; this gate compacts at a threshold and adds a cooldown. Caveats: the dispatch cold-starts claude and the hooks it installs are Claude Code hooks, so for our mixed seats the patterns transfer, not the package; comments and a few operator-facing strings, such as the staged-plan voice prompt contract, are Chinese in this first release; the README gives no threshold or cooldown values; Apache-2.0, 0 stars, created 2026-10-09; README-verified, not installed or run. entries.title: harness-creator — Claude Code plugin that turns repeated corrections in your own sessions into at most 3 proposed rules, hooks or skills a week, through five mostly code-run gates
entries.why: Claude Code plugin that reads your last 7 days of Claude Code sessions (Codex sessions too if you agree), finds repeated corrections, failure loops and repeated instructions, and proposes at most 3 rules, hooks or skills a week, each backed by quotes and session counts. Five gates, most of which run as plain code, not as another prompt, drop signals that were already resolved (G1), counts inflated by a single batch run (G2), issues that appeared only in Codex (G3, moved to a reference section), always-loaded rules with weak support (G4) and anything past the weekly limit of 3 (G5). The judge gets masked excerpts once, through your own claude CLI with no tools or MCP servers and your settings, CLAUDE.md, skills, plugins and hooks off (--restricted --safe-mode --tools ""), from an empty temporary folder. Rules, skills and hooks are written to ~/.claude only after you approve the diff, with a backup and undo; memory, script and agent ideas stay drafts. A rejected signal is not proposed again until it happens twice as often, and the next analysis reports whether an applied harness's signal came back. entries.title: claim-gate — Claude Code Stop hook that by default blocks, at most once per turn, a reply making a completion, count, absence or universal claim without the evidence its rule asks for
entries.why: Claude Code Stop hook in one standard-library Python file of about 270 lines; it does not judge whether a claim is true, only whether the reply shows how it was made. Five rules, each cleared by a command or a named line: completion ("all done", "tests pass") by a code block, a command or a Verified: line; number (a count or percentage stated as observed) by the command that produced it or a Counted with: line; absence ("nothing uses this") by two pieces of evidence (two commands or file:line citations) or a Searched: block; universal (all, every, none, always or never next to a countable noun) by a counted scope or a Scope: line; correction ("I was wrong" with a new number or cause) by a command, a file:line or a Correction source: line. Plans and questions do not fire, and text in code blocks, inline code and > quotes is ignored. In the default block mode the model is told which evidence to add; on the next stop of that turn Claude Code sets stop_hook_active and the hook passes, so it blocks at most once per turn; warn mode never blocks, and any internal error lets the stop through. 17 tests; each detector was replaced with always-fires and never-fires in turn, and all 10 broken versions turned at least one test red. Fit: a Verified: line is close to the VERIFIED field of our done receipt (only checks that ran, with evidence), and the absence rule sits next to our negative-claims rule; claimcheck, the source of our claim-vs-record rule, and proof-of-done check claims against the session transcript, while this reads only the final reply; the always-fires/never-fires check follows Kanon's K-PRIN-11 (a guard must be able to fail). Caveats: it checks for evidence, not for truth, since a reply can paste a command it never ran; English only and regex based, it misses claims phrased in ways its patterns do not cover and sometimes fires on descriptive sentences; evidence anywhere in the reply counts, so one command clears every number claim in the same reply, even claims it did not produce; MIT, 0 stars, created 2026-10-09; README-verified, not installed or run. entries.title: tamperproof — Claude Code plugin that blocks agent edits to existing test files, including through shell commands, and runs the tests when the agent stops with uncommitted changes
entries.why: Claude Code plugin of two plain-Node hooks with zero dependencies. PreToolUse on Edit, Write, MultiEdit, NotebookEdit and Bash blocks edits and overwrites of existing test files (exit 2, reason shown to the agent) and any shell command that names a test file unless it is a known read-only command or test runner, an allowlist so sed --in-place, node -e, python -c and redirects don't slip through; writing new test files is still allowed. The default protect list also covers snapshots and the places expected values hide (test/resources/, fixtures/, testdata/, golden/), and the config file protects itself. entries.title: dsh-goal-wait-gate — DSH plugin that by default withholds automatic goal continuation while the session still has a running or stopping background job or a live subagent
entries.why: DeepSeek Harness (DSH) plugin for a known, still-unfixed upstream behavior through DSH 0.2.1-alpha.1: the official driver injects a <goal_round> prompt whenever an agent is idle and its goal is active and armed, and idle only means no turn is running, so an agent that ended its turn to wait on a background job or subagent gets goal rounds that use up the round budget and re-prefill the whole session. Live work is a job the session owns in running or stopping status (read from ctx.jobs.list) or a live subagent descendant at any depth. entries.title: jev-belay — Claude Code Stop hook that reads the turn's transcript first and spends one Jev call only when files changed and no check has passed since
entries.why: Claude Code Stop hook (plugin or settings.json hook) for a final message that calls the work done when nothing backs it. It reads the transcript slice since the last prompt locally with two regex belts: a test, build or lint runner named in a command, and a runner's own summary in the output. If nothing changed, or a check passed after the last change, the hook exits and Jev is never asked. Only when something changed and nothing proved it does it send one jev-1.13.0 call with four questions, $0.00005 per call and 346 ms median latency; if the answer is an unverified done, it blocks the stop (exit 2) and Claude is told to run the tests, build or lint and report the actual result. Only the prompt, the closing message and two counts leave the machine. Blocks are capped at one per prompt, none within 60 seconds of the last and three per session; every error path exits 0; a shadow mode only reports what it would have blocked. entries.title: verified-ops-starter — freshness, no-op and rollout checks for scheduled jobs under one exit-code contract in which a dead checker cannot look like a clean result
entries.why: Python standard-library kit that replaces a scheduled job's self-report with evidence. freshness asks whether the job's real output is young enough (optional min_bytes, and a contains marker taken from the body, never the filename); wrap runs the job and announces a silent no-op when it exits 0 but its artifact did not change, comparing mtime and size, and kills and announces a hang under --timeout-s; rollout reads a fix back from each target, and a target whose verify only exits 0 comes back WEAK. One exit contract: 0 clean, 1 a problem found and the alert delivered, 3 found but the alert could not be delivered (also what --dry-run returns), 4 the checker itself died; a run that measured nothing, such as an empty or misspelled config, is 4, never 0, and under wrap any non-zero child code becomes 4 unless declared with --signal. selftest.py runs 44 checks, each first broken by a mutant, under the README's rule that a check with no mutant that makes it fail measures nothing. entries.title: Vigil — holds a scheduled agent's claim to independent checks you declare, reports a window nothing tried as missed and can re-run it, and flags identical output N runs in a row
entries.why: Python verification layer that supervises a scheduled job from outside and keeps two things apart: the claim, what the job says it did (JSON written to $VIGIL_CLAIM or one stdout line), and the check, evidence from outside the job (a file changed recently or has real content, an endpoint returns 200, a command passes, a metric went up). Verdicts: verified (exited 0 and the checks agree), unverified (exited 0, the evidence does not support it), failed (nonzero exit or timeout), missed (the window closed and nothing even tried), degraded (identical output N runs in a row, set by degrade_after). Schedules are declared in vigil.toml, which is how it can report a run that never happened; vigil catchup re-runs uncovered windows (the README's case: a laptop asleep through its 9:15 window); vigil run exits 0 on verified, 1 on failed and 2 on unverified or degraded; vigil check exits 1 if any job is missed, unverified or degraded. A job can also be watched without a command, checking only the artifact that window should have left. No daemon or database: it runs when the scheduler runs it and keeps one JSON state file; alerts are deduplicated per job. Fit: our Field Brief miss-watch (Collection's :44 catch-up when the :34 brief is missing) is the same missed-window idea for one routine; the README's demo bug, an except that returns an empty list so a dead source looks like a quiet day, is the case our negative-claims rule makes a gap. entries.title: brindle — milestones are done only when their checks exit 0, a new session re-runs checks rather than trust its status line, and autopilot resumes after a usage reset
entries.why: Supervisor that runs Claude Code, Codex, Google Antigravity and open-weight models side by side under tmux, each worker by default in its own git worktree and branch. A goal is split into milestones whose check commands brindle runs itself: a milestone is verified when its check exits 0, re-run after later merges, never when a model says so. The status lines it writes to goals.md are information only: a new session starts every milestone as pending and re-runs the checks. Under autopilot a branch merges only when a reviewer approved that exact commit (an approval carries over a clean merge of the base) and the checks pass, and a clean commit's passing result is cached by sha; manual merges are never gated. Autopilot stops when every milestone check passes and, by default, a read-only completion reviewer has audited the work against the goal and approved that commit, when it needs a decision, after three reminders with no progress, or near the Claude usage limit; there it pauses: the Claude workers stop, their worktrees, branches, queued messages and sessions are kept, and brindle restarts them after the reset; speaking to the supervisor doesn't end the pause. With plan_first a worker waits for plan approval, but only Claude workers are held by a hook (Edit, Write and NotebookEdit refused); other CLIs are only told to wait. entries.title: authority-demo — approval does not pre-approve the world: authority is re-checked at dispatch, and a signed finding records what the check read and whether it was writable
entries.why: Runnable demo for the Rigorix policy engine: a human approves an agent's payout, the beneficiary is frozen while the next run waits for approval, and once that run is approved the payout is refused at dispatch; the ledger never changes. Authority is checked when the agent asks and again immediately before the step executes, and the second check is the one that matters because it sees the current world; a beneficiary missing from the authority is refused even with an approval. The check is the whole policy: it answers one question and exits 0 to dispatch or 3 to refuse, with no LLM, no domain semantics and no network. The refusal is recorded in an HMAC-signed audit envelope with the outcome, exit code, checked_at, inputs_hash (the step inputs the engine fed the check), authority_digest (the authority content it read) and check_writable, which is true on the default $HOME install because your UID can write it. The rule the agent is judged by is not in its repository, and a PreToolUse hook denies direct payout, ledger and authority writes; the README calls this a policy + path + hook boundary, not a sandbox, since an unmediated write to $HOME is still possible. --isolated makes both files root-owned and non-writable, and setup refuses an agent user with passwordless sudo unless overridden with a loud warning. Fit: a re-check at dispatch for anything approved before it runs; Titan's verifier-outside-the-repo rule, applied to authority; and evidence for our done receipt's VERIFIED line: what the check read, when, and whether the guard was writable. Caveats: needs rigorix-mcp 1.9.2+ and Node 22+; no LICENSE file (GitHub reports none), so treat it as all rights reserved and as pattern only: read and re-implement the idea; copy no file and vendor no code; 0 stars, created 2026-10-06; README-verified, not installed or run. entries.title: Kanon — agent-workflow rulebook: a guard must be able to fail, a detector reports what it examined, and there is no configuration to switch a rule off
entries.why: Opinionated workflow for GitHub and Claude Code in which agents file, implement and review work under a rulebook of about 200 rules, each with its reason. Two principles are why it is here. K-PRIN-11, a guard must be able to fail: mutation-check every guard assertion by breaking the thing it protects and confirming it goes red, separately for each assertion; when a mutation passes, decide whether it is equivalent or the assertion is dead; scope a documentation guard to the line or block that makes the claim and make it throw when its anchor moves; restore a mutated file from a copy, never by reverting it to the committed version, which reverts the fix too. K-PRIN-8: every detector reports a coverage figure (what it examined), not only what it found, and a check whose healthy state is silence emits a positive signal that it ran. K-PRIN-9 records a missing measurement as absent, never as zero, and K-PRIN-1 gives a reason for having no configuration: a guard that checks the code against a config the code also reads can no longer fail. Fit: a test procedure behind our negative-claims rule (a failed lookup is a gap, never zero) and code decides done, next to Ruttla's two-probe rule and corralai's planted faults. Caveats: by its own Enforced-by lines K-PRIN-11 is only partly enforced (the brief guard is mutation-tested, elsewhere prose only), K-PRIN-8 per component with no general guard, and K-PRIN-1 prose only, so these are mostly prose rules; it assumes GitHub Actions and Claude Code as its runtimes, so only the rules transfer; pre-1.0, Apache-2.0, 0 stars, created 2026-09-30; README and rulebook/00-principles.md verified, not installed or run. entries.title: vibeguard — one Rust hook runtime for Codex, Claude Code and Grok: blocks a few destructive commands, records outcomes not commands, checks push ancestry
entries.why: Rust CLI (v2) with native hooks for Codex, Claude Code or Grok (written to $GROK_HOME/hooks for Grok), plus a DSH Bash adapter that routes blocks through DSH's native approval and fails closed if the pre-call runtime fails. The result hook keeps only the latest outcome, optional exit code, timestamp, cwd and tool-use ID, never the raw command or output. An explicit per-repo pre-push hook rejects remote ref deletion and tag replacement, requires fast-forward branch updates, and makes missing objects an explicit error. entries.title: TokenPilot — PATH launchers wrap installed coding CLIs to count tokens locally, with no proxy, a bypass, and no savings claimed from session counters

entries.title: tmux-agent-status — Claude Code and Codex status from the agents' own session state, not hooks, so an Esc interrupt doesn't leave a window stuck on working
entries.why: tmux plugin that shows each coding agent's status in the window list from the agent's own on-disk session state instead of agent hooks. Hook trackers set working on submit and done on Stop, but an Esc interrupt fires no hook, so the window stays on working. For the claude CLI it reads ~/.claude/sessions/<pid>.json, whose status (busy, idle, waiting or shell) Claude updates on every transition, interrupts included. entries.title: Ruttla — deterministic quality gate: every rule must fail its broken probe and pass its healthy one, and exit 2 means nothing was measured
entries.why: Local quality gate that turns a proven failure into an executable rule: a rule must fail its broken probe and pass its healthy probe, and ruttla --self-test re-runs both. The exit code is a contract: 0 measured with no blocking finding, 1 a blocking finding, 2 nothing was measured (the README says not a success), 3 a runner, input, config or plugin error. Without its engine the declarative rules report as unmeasured, never green, and platforms with no rule pack are listed instead of passing. The README warns that ruttla . | head reports head's status, so capture the code before filtering. --format agent prints one line per finding with a FIX: hint; scans use no LLM or network and never execute target code. Fit: it puts our negative-claim rule and code decides done into an exit code a wrapper can test, and its two-probe test is an admission rule for checks we add. entries.title: sandbox-run — verify in a detached worktree overlaid by manifest copy, then check the main tree's VCS state stayed byte-identical
entries.why: Runs build, test or lint commands in a detached git worktree (or jj workspace) in a temp directory, not the live checkout. Uncommitted files are overlaid by manifest copy, never patch-apply, hardlink or symlink, so writes cannot leak back, and cache directories such as target/ and node_modules/ are left out, so a pass comes from a clean rebuild and catches a forgotten new file the way CI would. Timeouts kill the whole process group. The isolation.integrity gate checks that the main tree's VCS state is byte-identical before and after (failure exits 2). By default, sandbox.clean marks a run that changed the snapshot as polluted, and runs are logged to the append-only .sandbox-run/runs.jsonl. Fit: our wrapper fails a push-required kick on a dirty tree (no-exit-while-waiting), and the README's first problem is build artifacts mixing into the change set; it isolates only the verify step. Caveats: the ledger is the one file it writes in the main tree, so .sandbox-run/ needs a .gitignore line; a large project's first run rebuilds caches slowly; Rust CLI; 0 stars, MIT, created 2026-08-20; README-verified, not installed or run. entries.title: Tenex (Jake Klaristenfeld) — eval-driven development: graders on traces, promotion, k-run bars
entries.why: Tenex guide to eval-driven development: an eval is a grader applied to a trace, with case (dataset item) and run (experiment) completing the vocabulary; maps the names across LangSmith, Langfuse, Braintrust and Arize AX/Phoenix (names shift fast, check current docs). What connects online and offline evals is promotion: turning a bad production trace into an offline regression case (scrub sensitive data first). Loop: define case + pass criteria, watch it fail, change the agent, rerun, then run the full dataset for regressions. K-run bars: all-of-k for high-stakes behavior — passing k-of-k doesn't prove it can't happen, failing once proves it can — or n-of-k like 2-of-3. LLM judges need checking: label a few dozen cases by hand, measure agreement, fix the rubric before scores drive decisions, recheck on every judge change. Grade the path early: add at least one trajectory grader from the start, not just the final answer. What to try here: promote failed done-receipt runs into the replay set as regression cases; calibrate any judge before its scores gate a promotion; keep one trajectory check on Coding EM slices. Already covered in parts: Three-Run Proof, replay set, detection floor, disproof review (https://caohy1988.github.io/research/harness/#three-run-proof) and the 2026-10-04 @sermakarevich Lab cards (failure taxonomy / replay set / worst-of-three, judge calibration). Its replay benchmark scores routers on your own dispatch history against the dumbest baseline: a keyword rule (89%) beat an LLM classifier (84%). entries.title: Titan Receipts + POAW — a receipt only counts if the party it describes can't verify it, and a claim that is only local is not evidence
entries.why: Titan gives every commit a hash-chained, HMAC-signed receipt (model, Claude Code version, session, file and diff hashes), verifiable offline. Its CI check runs its own pinned verifier, never the copy committed in the repo under audit, because the party who could alter receipts also controls a vendored verifier; the escape hatch warns that the result is then self-reported. /verify-chain ends with an ANCHOR count of untracked, uncommitted or unpushed receipts, a keyless clone says SIGNATURES NOT CHECKED and exits 2, and the README spells out what a receipt proves and what it doesn't. POAW / qed-proof-core (https://github.com/Nuraveda/qed-proof-core) adds the destination check: when an agent claims a push, the node asks GitHub and signs a pass or Failed receipt into an append-only Merkle log. Fits our gap-not-zero and VERIFIED-means-ran receipt locks, which today are self-administered, and the no-exit-while-waiting push rule. Caveats: Titan 1 star, MIT, HMAC is a shared secret; POAW 3 stars, Apache-2.0 spec plus AGPL-3.0 node, so patterns only and copy nothing, and it was read at headline level; README-verified, not run. Documentation pattern, no new seat, no Herdr. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: bastionfuse — containment that never reads text: honeytokens, decoys, taint-then-egress, and a sticky per-session fuse
entries.why: Starts from the case we never write down, that the model itself is the attacker, so it relies only on controls outside the LLM. It plants honeytokens, decoy files and decoy MCP tools, matches tokens in call inputs and in results across common encodings, and taints a session that reads a decoy; after that, any data-capable call trips the fuse. That catches curl -d @.env.backup even though the secret never appears in the arguments. Trips are sticky and per session, a bounded trace is kept, the guard protects its own state and settings, and the state path is baked into the hook. Rollout: operator-written rules enforce from day one, while built-in budgets only log 'would trip' until real sessions are reviewed, which is a clean statement of our shadow-to-active ladder. Fills a gap next to coding-agent-guardrails and Preflight, which prevent or declare but have no canary. Caveats are the README's own: tamper-evident, not tamper-proof, against a same-user agent; a hook that can't start fails open; /clear or deleting state resets it; shell egress detection is word-based; about 250 ms per tool call; 0 stars, MIT, created the day it was collected; README-verified, not run. Reference only; any live-seat hook needs Haiyuan. No new seat, no Herdr. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: cache-live-control — prompt-cache TTL as a per-chat decision, with the agent's wait and delegation rule priced against it
entries.why: Claude Code plugin whose /cache command switches the main-chat and subagent TTLs separately, mid-session, at no cost. It publishes the TTL source-precedence table (FORCE_PROMPT_CACHING_5M down to automatic: 1h on a subscription, 5m on an API key or cloud provider) and notes that subagents default to 5m even when the main chat is on 1h. Its new idea is a priced-wait rule: on a 1h cache, delegate anything past roughly 30 tool calls and wait, because waiting is free and writes cost 2x; on 5m, work directly and keep each wait under 4 minutes. It also names the transcript fields that make cache claims checkable (message.usage.cache_creation ephemeral_5m / ephemeral_1h input tokens, with subagent messages under subagents/), and reports 11 of 12 warm TTL switches kept the cache. Adds the missing decision to our cache lane (cachebeat, cache-keepalive, contextscope, stable-context-first measure or reorder; none picks the TTL). Caveats: built on early-access function hooks; it can't see the plan, so it assumes the longer TTL; the measurement is the author's own 12 runs; 1 star, MIT; README-verified, not installed. entries.title: corralai — critic must differ from writer, unreproduced review claims are demoted, mutation kill-rate measures test adequacy (patterns only)
