entries.title: everyhook: one hook source translated per coding agent, benched before install
entries.why: Zero-dependency Node tool (Node 18 or newer) with one hook contract and one adapter per agent for five coding agents that, per the README, agree on almost nothing: the pre-tool event is PreToolUse, BeforeTool or preToolUse, the refusal is spelled four ways, ask works in two, timeouts are seconds in four and milliseconds in one, exit code 2 blocks in four but not in one of them on Windows, where a shell layer turns it into 1, and exit code 1 denies in only one. run, the adapter, reads the agent's own JSON, builds one document for your hook, runs it and prints the agent's own JSON back; an answer an agent cannot take (an ask for an agent that has none, a deny at an event that cannot refuse) is translated to the nearest thing it can take, and bench and explain say which. install and uninstall edit each agent's config textually with that agent's event names, matcher and timeout unit, after a backup, adding only their own entries, and uninstall leaves the file byte for byte as it was. bench runs your hook against 64 documents, 53 recorded from four of the agents' real binaries plus 11 for the fifth written from its reference, and prints what the hook answered, what the agent would do and the exact JSON; explain marks every statement binary (a real run saw it) or docs (the reference says so). The author's evidence: the four binaries run on Windows 11 on 2026-10-17, CI on Windows, macOS and Linux runners on every push, and a 180-case translation table (5 agents × 6 events × 6 answers) pinned by tests. The gap is stated throughout: the fifth agent's binary was never run (its CLI needs a login), so every statement about it is docs and its fixtures say documented, not recorded. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, we run six Mac CLI seats (#roster) and mirror the same guards by hand on each (force-push blocks, env-file protection, tool logging), so a guard fixed on one seat and silently missing on another is our standing failure mode. everyhook supplies the missing portability layer: one hook source, translation per seat, and a bench meant to show that the same hook means the same thing on each seat before it is installed. The pack reads the byte-preserving uninstall and the binary-versus-docs tags as matching our reversibility and observed-versus-claimed rules, and places it beside kept rollcage-guard (one guard's rules) at a distribution layer no kept card covers. We already have: a fleet-wide installer that wires the vault's contract file and skills into the seats' homes (#skills); the always-on play of skills for advisory policy and hooks for must-hold rules, no secrets in the diff, no push to main and no weakening tests during a fix among them (#em-loop); a run-log lesson in which one plugin's pre- and post-tool-use hooks hung 1.5 to 6+ minutes per tool call and stalled two runs (#mac-run-lessons); GREEN, YELLOW and RED tiers by reversibility, with park-and-ask for anything that cannot be undone in under a minute (#gyr-authority), and a promotion gate that needs a rollback actually tried once (#promotion-gate); a completion claim that counts only when the session record backs it (#claim-vs-record), and Lab cards that call a practice applied only where this playbook says so (#lab-card-claims); and the rule that a new check is first seen to fail on a deliberately broken input and that a pass says what it examined (#check-can-fail). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): fleet guards (force-push, env-file, tool log) written once against one contract and translated per seat instead of hand-mirrored copies; a bench-only trial of our existing guards against recorded documents for two of our seats' agents before any install, with the bench output (the answer, the agent's effect and the exact JSON) required in the change packet; binary-versus-docs basis tags on every hook-behavior claim in our playbook; and byte-preserving uninstall, checked byte for byte, as the rollback standard. Installing it on live seats would edit their config, so that is a separate Haiyuan decision. Caveats: the fifth agent is entirely unverified (docs only); the real-binary evidence is Windows-first, CI covers macOS and Linux, and our Mac seats would be the trial; answers an agent cannot express are degraded to the nearest one, so the degradation has to be read guard by guard; the binary runs, the 64 bench documents and the 180-case table are the author's, read in the README, not re-run; MIT, 1 star, created 2026-10-17; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: agent-role-contracts: offline preflight that rejects self-review and stale handoffs
entries.why: Deterministic, offline preflight (Node 22.5 or newer; no API key, runtime or account) over a declared role, permissions, work scope and handoff. Before anything executes it rejects, each with a specific diagnostic: a task requesting a write outside its declared authority; implementer and reviewer collapsing into one declared role (self-review); a reviewed task or action that changed afterward (stale subject binding: the G1 digest covers the full bundle, policy, roles and routes included, plus the full task and the declared action, and a review or approval must bind that current digest); a filesystem mapping drifting from the declared action (the G2 filesystem-write adapter takes exactly a path and a content SHA-256 and rejects unknown parameters); and stale lifecycle or handoff declarations. Every result states that a PASS is not execution authority: it means the declarations are internally consistent under the checks that ran, while runtime identity, actual permissions, side-effect enforcement, evidence verification and execution approval remain separate and are stated as false. The digest gives integrity, not authenticity or authorization, and artifact paths and URLs are not immutable evidence. The author marks it stable 1.0.0 (npm latest, verified 2026-10-16), keeping the 0.5.0 public imports, API shapes, twelve schema identities, fail-closed claims and G1 digests, with a compatibility corpus that requires every other machine-report field, schema byte, fixed digest and raw CLI output to stay equal; the schema engine is a closed Draft-07 subset in which unsupported keywords fail loudly. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our chief-of-staff rooms and EM loop enforce implementer ≠ reviewer and task scope by prompt and by human reading, the layer that drifts when a handoff goes stale or a task is re-pointed after review. This moves three checks before execution and into code: scope against authority, role separation, and review bound to a digest, so that changing the task after review means the approval no longer matches. The pack calls that last rule the mechanical form of our dual-LGTM intent, stated more crisply than in any kept card, and places the checker beside kept agent-delegate-class handoff patterns and plan-validation (plan rehearsal), at a declaration layer neither checks. We already have: an EM loop in which the agent that wrote the code cannot approve it and the implementer is never a reviewer on the same PR (#em-loop); review verdicts pinned to the head SHA, where a line naming an older SHA is UNPARSED and dual LGTM means two APPROVE lines on the current head SHA (#review-verdict-line); an approval re-check right before a RED action runs, confirming that the action still matches the approved item and that current authority still permits it, as policy text only (#approval-recheck); a machine-readable handoff packet (from, to, job_type, objective, artifacts, decisions, constraints, open questions, next gate) whose completeness check is shadow only and never blocks (#handoff-packet); and RED actions such as send or publish, spend, merge, permissions and production, which always go to Haiyuan (#gyr-authority). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): EM and chief-of-staff handoff packets that carry a declared role, permissions, work scope and reviewer, checked offline before a seat starts, with a write outside scope and an implementer who is also the reviewer both rejected; review and approval bound to a digest of the full bundle, task and action, so any change after review invalidates the approval until it is re-reviewed; and every PASS labeled declarations-consistent only, with execution authority, identity, enforcement and evidence verification kept as separate gates. The pack frames the trial as one EM flow with an offline check only and no control change; making it a gate on live handoffs would be a separate Haiyuan decision. Caveats: production adoption is not claimed by the author; the filesystem adapter covers exactly one operation (write_file with a path and content SHA-256), so broader tool semantics would need our own adapters; digests give integrity, not authenticity; the compatibility corpus is the author's, read in the README, not re-run; MIT, 1 star, created 2026-09-30; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: pinwash: post-session diff check for weakened pins, hooks and required checks
entries.why: Local-first, deterministic checker (Python 3.11 or newer, standard library only at scan time; no model, no network) that asks one question of a Git diff: did this change make an agent more able to claim done by weakening pins, hooks, permissions, required checks or bypass instructions? It does not execute the subject and enforces nothing. A session starts with pinwash session start in a clean worktree before the agent begins, and pinwash session review runs once the agent and every process it started have stopped; it asks, and a trusted controller passes --stopped only after making sure of that itself, since pinwash neither stops processes nor verifies that they stopped. The review runs three comparisons against the pinned baseline and the saved judge identity and writes a JSON report outside the project; each finding says what changed, why it matters and what to review next, and no findings does not prove that verification runs or that the product works. Verdicts are exact: Pass when all three invocations are clean; Held when they are clean except for an EXEMPTION_ADDED, meaning the session wrote an exemption record that only human review releases; Block on any exit 1; and anything else (exit 2, a timeout, unparseable output) is not judged, never a pass. Exemptions are per finding fingerprint and live on the base side only, with six required keys, an expiry no more than 180 days after creation and never a rule glob, and the exemption channel never exempts its own findings. The author reports that both installed wheels passed 690 tests in local Docker Linux verification, with a public acceptance receipt and frozen acceptance fixtures A1–A11, and states the limits plainly: Windows and macOS are not yet validated (package acceptance is Docker Linux only, and byte-identical JSON across platforms is specified but not CI-verified), and there is no 1.0 stability claim. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our agents can edit the very hooks and checks that judge them, and pinwash checks whether an agent edited the checks: gutted a hook into a non-stub that can no longer block, dropped a required context, or committed an exemption that quietly drops a finding once merged. The pack reads base-side-only exemptions plus Held-means-human-release as the right governance shape for a fleet whose agents can edit their own harness files, and the tool as directly trial-shaped, a post-session diff review on one seat's worktree. We already have: a test-tamper scan in which the EM and each reviewer read a code change's diff for tests skipped, deleted or focused, gutted assertions or a test command changed so it always passes, a green run after such a change being SUSPECT, never PASS; it is a prose rule with no hook installed, and no tamper incident is traced in our records yet (#claim-vs-record); the same scan also looks for || true added after a check and for commits made with --no-verify, which skips the repo's hooks, and a check that examined nothing is a gap under NOT VERIFIED, never a pass (#check-can-fail); blind reviewers who scan code diffs for test tampering while attempting disproof (#disproof-review); hooks for must-hold rules, no weakening tests during a fix among them (#em-loop); and the rule that killing a stale session does not prove the old agent stopped, so a resume waits until the old process is confirmed gone, checked by hand (#watchdog-resume-safety), the same assurance pinwash leaves to a trusted controller before --stopped. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): agent sessions on harness-bearing repos run against a pinned baseline, a snapshot at session start and then a post-session review asking only whether pins, hooks, permissions or required checks were weakened; exemptions kept on the base side only, per finding fingerprint with an expiry of at most 180 days, and any exemption a session adds holding the work for human release; and a checker failure (a timeout, unparseable output, exit 2) treated as not judged, never a pass, and surfaced as a gap, not a zero. The pack frames the trial as report-only on one worktree, with the JSON report kept outside the project; using its verdicts to hold or block live work would be a separate Haiyuan decision. Caveats: Alpha 0.1.1 (SPEC 29) with no 1.0 claim; macOS and Windows are unvalidated, so a trial on our Mac would itself be the platform test; unknown_coverage rows need a local policy or they turn into noise, since ignored local settings files and hook logs surface every session; the 690 tests and the acceptance receipt are the author's, read in the README, not re-run; MIT, 0 stars, created 2026-09-28; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: fael: per-file continuity ledger in .git, surfaced when the file is next touched
entries.why: Continuity ledger for agent work (an npm package for three coding-agent CLIs and MCP) that files each note where the code is touched and returns it where the code is touched. A hand-off written with fael add note, naming files (--files) and a key (--key), reaches the next session when it opens that file or its prompt names the key; an assignment, to a person by git user.name or to an agent, lists in full at that seat's session start, and the receipt prints the line to paste plus the command that starts the other agent on the row; fael never wakes an agent, and the row is read when the agent next starts or touches the file. fael claim <id> shows (held @<branch>) so a parallel agent picks something else, a signal and never a lock. Requirements and decisions written once reach every later agent that touches that code, and --revisit resurfaces a row when it is due. Its behavior rules: writing costs no extra turn (the agent runs fael add in the same message as its next tool call, or ends a reply with fael decision, issue or note lines that fael files without stopping the turn); reading and searching bring nothing, because rows wait for the edit, so a sub-agent with empty context gets the memory its brief left out at the file it edits; and rows are pushed per file once per context window (re-told after compaction) and cut to a token budget (800 by default) rather than dumped as notes. Rows retire once the code absorbs them (git owns what changed; fael keeps only what git cannot say), and fael stats and fael report show exactly what was put into context (handed over against acted on, retired at touch, handoffs picked up, across agents), under the standing line that fael never claims what it cannot measure. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our written handoffs (chief-of-staff packets, EM intent, spec and plan, vault notes) are addressed to tasks, while fael addresses memory to files, where the next seat actually looks. The pack says three mechanisms carry over even without adoption: push on edit only, with no summary stuffed in before the agent says what it will do (the README's critique of summary memory is that it averages away the one row that mattered); a claim as a signal, not a lock, for parallel worktrees; and retire-when-absorbed plus measured pickup, so the ledger cannot rot into stale notes that still get injected. The pack places it beside kept pair-mailbox (seat-to-seat delivery) and the vault (durable decisions), at the in-repo, per-file layer neither covers. We already have: handoffs that pass ownership, not transcripts, through a machine-readable packet, the artifact carrying the detail and the packet the state (#handoff-packet); intent.md, spec.md and plan.md kept next to the code with git history as the audit trail (one SDK repo keeps them in the vault or local-only), and review fix passes that append a short record to plan.md instead of silently rewriting it (#em-loop); every coding stage filing vault notes so the next agent inherits state (#coding); recall that greps the notes' one-line summaries, written with the exact names a later search would use (a file path among them), and opens only the notes that apply (#memory-loop); two clocks, with fast-changing facts re-fetched live before any action or claim rather than remembered (#memory-rules); a byte ceiling on the policy files every agent reads before every task, because every task pays the full read (#resident-budget); and the rule that a count in a receipt, Decision or Lab card names how it was counted and over what (#check-can-fail). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): a trial of file-scoped notes, decisions and issues in one active repo, written in the same turn as the work, pushed only when that file is edited, within an 800-token budget and re-told after compaction; parallel-worktree coordination by claim as a signal (held @<branch>), never a lock; and rows that retire when the code absorbs them, with fael-stats-style pickup accounting (handed over against acted on, the across-agents count) as required reporting, so an unmeasured memory claim is not accepted. The pack frames it as a one-repo trial with stats reported weekly, removing the ledger as the rollback and the vault untouched; note that its rows retire automatically, whereas our memory loop deletes durable lessons only after Haiyuan approves the specific items (#memory-loop). Caveats: young, created 2026-09-24; the pickup metrics are the author's definitions until our trial reproduces them; per-file push needs tuning so hot files do not become a new context tax; fael never wakes an agent, so delivery waits for the next start or touch and urgent handoffs still need the chief-of-staff packet; MIT, 1 star; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: handoff-bus: main-to-line message bus whose line names survive replaced conversations
entries.why: Small zero-dependency host plugin (Node built-ins only) for the coding-agent harness that one of our seats runs: it lets a main conversation and the GUI sub-conversations you open yourself send each other instructions and reports directly through bus_send, with a target and a kind, so the operator stops switching windows to relay. Three-level addressing (main, a line such as api, and temporary conversations api.1 and api.2) means replacing a conversation never changes what main writes: a message lands on whichever conversation under that line is alive. The bus is scoped by the session's working directory, one independent bus per workspace. It has three remembered behaviors: a start-up briefing in every new conversation, a context-watermark notice at 40%, and a refusal to unregister without writing the ledger. Its boundaries are explicit: it does not create or close conversations (you open them; it only registers and routes them and emits suggestHandoff), does not compress context, does no file watching, polling or autonomous work, and does not replace state files (it delivers short pointers and wakes the target, while authoritative content stays in files); there is no cross-workspace addressing, and subagent sessions cannot be addressed (only a top-level GUI conversation can be a target; otherwise bus_send answers target_unresolvable). It needs a web or desktop profile with the host's session controller and session store, and headless or SDK-only profiles leave it inactive. The author tested it on that harness's 0.2.0-rc.x desktop build on Windows, against internal APIs (sessionController.resolveAgent, agent.followup/inject, sessions.flush, agent/created, agent/pre-step) that are not a public contract, so a future release may require a patch; if a hook throws, it degrades to no advisory and the turn proceeds untouched. Tool-result and relay bodies are in Chinese; error codes are stable English identifiers. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, it directly serves a seat we pin, which three kept cards already extend (the newest kept 10-18), and the pack counts that seat as our most actively extended one, whose handoffs still need window-switching relays. The adoptable shape, per the pack, is a stable line name over replaceable conversations, pointers rather than payloads, and an unregister that requires the ledger: the handoff discipline our written packets keep by convention, here enforced at the bus. We already have: that seat on the hourly collect rotation and as an optional implementer (#roster), with the shared contract and skills wired into its home (#skills); handoffs that pass ownership, not transcripts, the artifact carrying the detail and the packet the state (#handoff-packet), where a missing packet field on a new kick gets a note and never blocks it (#coding-em-kicks); a post-task vault note that stays mandatory as proof of done, as policy text that nothing enforces (#memory-loop); and continuity through each tool's session id, reused per PR or slice instead of cold-starting follow-ups (#launch), with the quota-failover handoff still the named session id plus a vault note (#exception-first). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): a trial of main-to-line routing on that seat, in which main addresses a line name, the bus lands it on the live conversation, and a takeover (api.1 to api.2) never changes main's addressing; bus messages that carry only a summary and file pointers, with authoritative content staying in files; and the three remembered behaviors (start-up briefing, 40% watermark notice, no unregister without the ledger) along with the hard boundaries (the bus never creates or closes conversations, never addresses subagent sessions, and runs one bus per workspace). The pack frames it as a one-seat trial pinned to a reviewed SHA, with removing the plugin as the rollback. Caveats: per the pack, our pinned version on macOS is unverified, since the author tested only the Windows desktop 0.2.0-rc.x build, and the internal-API basis has to be pinned to a reviewed SHA, with a patch expected per release; the playbook launches every long Mac CLI run, that seat's collect included, through a tmux wrapper (#launch), while the bus stays inactive on headless profiles, so whether any of our runs has the profile it needs is unverified; relay bodies are in Chinese; nothing has been measured here; MIT, 0 stars, created 2026-10-18; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: Meta Engineering, 'The Thin Orchestrator' — deterministic rule-table router in front of Jev, which handles only the cases the table does not cover
entries.why: Meta's engineering post 'The Thin Orchestrator: How We Made Our AI Agents More Reliable by Giving the Router Less to Do' (engineering.fb.com, 2026-10-19; Plawan Rath, Akhil Jindal and Ashwini Verma) describes a 1,300-line orchestrator that routes 20+ workflows to 14 specialist subagents and does zero domain work itself. Every request follows a fixed 7-step protocol: read the subagent's instruction file, check whether the target already exists, gather required fields from the user, auto-discover what can be inferred, run a reliability gate for active warnings or required reviewers, delegate to the subagent with full context, and handle results (surface errors, confirm success); steps 1–5 and 7 are deterministic, and only step 6 uses LLM reasoning, inside an isolated subagent with only its domain knowledge loaded. Every subagent follows one standard structure (knowledge sources, a pre-gathering checklist, a step-by-step workflow, discovery patterns, troubleshooting), and workflow templates fix the order in which specialists run, so a new use case, pipeline migration, needed a new template and zero new agent code. Reported results: configuration prep for a new column took three to four days by hand and about a day with their earlier config-driven system, and takes under an hour with the thin orchestrator; about two-thirds of the system's changes land without significant human edits. This card takes the router. The post's rule: 'which subagent handles this?' is a routing decision, not a reasoning task, so routing stays deterministic (keyword matching, intent classification, field gathering) and the line between deterministic and probabilistic work is drawn explicitly. Why it matters here: Jev, our typed decision layer (Choice / Score / Noul answers through the TypeSafe API, on OpenRouter typesafe/jev-1.13, mode active since 2026-09-20), takes typed state through jev-route or jev-shadow and answers its gates (intake, pre_browser, pre_retry, pre_research, pre_tool, and worth_running in shadow); a caller honors an answer only at confidence ≥ the 0.55 floor in router.json and otherwise falls back to CoS. The idea: a deterministic rule table in front of Jev, run on the same typed state, where a matching row returns its answer with no model call and only states that no row covers go to Jev, under the unchanged floor and CoS fallback. Our own baseline points the same way: on 2026-09-27, worth_running said run on 139 of 142 answered calls, and a Jev gate goes shadow → active only if it beats that always-majority constant (#constant-baseline), plus the replay check and Three-Run Proof; a rule table writes such constants down as rows instead of paying a model call for each. We already have, as Lab cards only: bouncer's card, whose hard rules and fast-path allowlist decide tool calls in code before its Jev questions run, and downshift's card, deterministic subagent model routing with no model in the loop; this card applies the same edges-in-code split to our own Jev routing. Status: trial idea, not installed and not scheduled; router.json, Jev's mode and its kill switch do not change; any install or adoption needs Haiyuan, and promoting any gate from shadow to active still needs Haiyuan's approval plus the replay check, constant baseline and Three-Run Proof. Card requested by Haiyuan on 2026-10-20. Caveats: the post's numbers are Meta's own, from one data-pipeline system (column onboarding across three code repositories, three programming languages and up to six pipeline stages), and none has been measured here; no rule table exists, so how many of our calls it would cover is unknown (139 of 142 is one gate's answers, not a routing count). Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: Meta Engineering, 'The Thin Orchestrator' — checks before every handoff: does the target already exist, and are there active warnings or required reviewers?
entries.why: Meta's engineering post 'The Thin Orchestrator' (engineering.fb.com, 2026-10-19) describes a 1,300-line orchestrator that routes 20+ workflows to 14 specialist subagents through a fixed 7-step protocol in which steps 1–5 and 7 are deterministic and only step 6 uses LLM reasoning, and reports that configuration prep for a new column fell from three to four days by hand to under an hour. This card takes two of the deterministic steps that run before every delegation: step 2 checks whether the target already exists, to prevent duplicates, and step 5 is a reliability gate that checks for active warnings or required reviewers. The post's argument: a heavyweight orchestrator that hallucinates routes to the wrong agent, gathers the wrong fields or skips reliability checks, while a thin one follows a fixed protocol. Why it matters here: every handoff from Manage to a specialist, and every new Coding EM kick row, carries a machine-readable packet (from, to, job_type, objective, artifacts, decisions, constraints, open_questions, next_gate), and its completeness check, Jev packet_complete, is shadow only and never blocks (#handoff-packet). We already have parts of it: Collection URL-dedupes the extra collect packs before each deep brief; publishing has one owner, Collection, with miss-watch as a catch-up rather than a second publisher; an ambiguous route goes to Haiyuan, never a silent misroute; an approval re-check runs right before a RED action, as policy text only (#approval-recheck); and, as a Lab card only, agent-role-contracts' offline preflight rejects self-review and stale handoffs. Status: trial idea, not installed and not scheduled; no handoff contract, skill or playbook text changes; any install or adoption needs Haiyuan. Card requested by Haiyuan on 2026-10-20. Caveats: the post's numbers are Meta's own, from one data-pipeline system, and none has been measured here; what counts as the same work for the duplicate check, and where active warnings are read from, would need defining before any trial. entries.title: Meta Engineering, 'The Thin Orchestrator' — named workflow templates: set orders of specialists reused across workflows
entries.why: Meta's engineering post 'The Thin Orchestrator' (engineering.fb.com, 2026-10-19) describes a 1,300-line orchestrator that routes 20+ workflows to 14 specialist subagents through a fixed 7-step protocol in which steps 1–5 and 7 are deterministic and only step 6 uses LLM reasoning, and reports that configuration prep for a new column fell from three to four days by hand to under an hour. This card takes the workflow templates: deterministic state machines that constrain the LLM's decision space by fixing the phase order, such as Column Onboarding (Schema → Validation → Population → Testing), Event Onboarding (Schema → Population → Validation → Testing → Event Processing) and Pipeline Migration (Assessment → Planning → Population → Validation → Monitoring). All three reuse the same pool of 14 subagents in different orders; pipeline migration, a completely new use case, took a new template and zero new agent code, and the post's first question for any new use case is 'Can I sequence existing agents differently?' Why it matters here: we already run set orders of seats, but they live in separate locks and cards rather than under one name. The Field Brief runs the 3-way hourly collect (Agy, Muse and DSH by hour % 3) and two extra collect seats, Collection URL-dedupes the extra packs before the 12h deep brief (00:34 / 12:34 PT), and Collection publishes; a coding job runs the Opus 5.5 implementer, then blind review in which the implementer is never a reviewer on the same PR (#em-loop), then fix rounds capped at three before escalating (Haiyuan 2026-10-20 02:39 PT), then Haiyuan's merge gate. The idea is named workflow templates: each set order written once under a name (for example field-brief or code-pr) and cited by the handoffs that run it, so that a new use case is first tried as a new order of existing seats, in line with the 'No new seat.' line our Lab cards keep. Status: trial idea, not installed and not scheduled; no routine, schedule, skill or handoff contract changes; any install or adoption needs Haiyuan. Card requested by Haiyuan on 2026-10-20. Caveats: the post's numbers are Meta's own, from one data-pipeline system, and none has been measured here; Meta's templates order specialists inside one domain, while our seats are general CLIs and Grok bots, so the reuse may be smaller; field-brief and code-pr are example names, not agreed ones. entries.title: A public agent-workflow plugin guide (pstack, Oct 2026) — pair each rule with what enforces it, rank fixes by how well they hold, and show every new check failing on a past mistake
entries.why: A public agent-workflow plugin guide (pstack, Oct 2026) teaches its plugin in ten chapters. Chapter 9, 'Make it yours' (section 'Fix the environment with /correct'), says that when agents are corrected for the same mistake again and again, the fix belongs in the repo, not in the next prompt, and ranks the options by how well they hold: (1) make the mistake impossible with architecture or a better data structure; (2) block it with types, or with a lint or CI check whose error names the fix; (3) catch it with a test; (4) write it down as a doc or agent rule, last, because nothing fails when an agent skips a rule. Human review is not on the list: a reviewer who must catch the same mistake on every PR is the problem the fix removes. Its /correct skill reads recent commits, reverts, review comments and comments that explain workarounds, groups the mistakes into classes (a class counts once it has happened twice), fixes the most frequent classes one commit each at the highest level that works, proves each new check fails on a real past mistake, and keeps a table in the agent instruction file that pairs each rule with what enforces it, so that a rule nothing enforces shows up as a repeat. Chapter 8 names the principle, Encode Lessons in Structure: advice repeated twice becomes a lint, check or script. Why it matters here: our AGENTS.md states its rules as text, and our repeat-lesson rule (#repeat-lesson) already turns a lesson that is in forbidden.md twice into a proposed fix where the rule is applied (skill text, an instruction-file line, a prompt block or a checker/hook spec) instead of another paragraph; the playbook records 18 near-identical blind-review preflight paragraphs (2026-09-20 to 09-24) that never became a filter, and forbidden.md now sits exactly at its 81,155 B ceiling (#resident-budget). The idea: (a) one table that pairs every AGENTS.md rule with its enforcer, so that the policy-only rules are visible; (b) when a repeat lesson's fix is drafted, rank the options in the guide's order and say why a higher level did not work; (c) a new check counts once it has failed on the real past mistake that prompted it (the forbidden.md incident or the failed receipt). #check-can-fail already asks for a deliberately broken input (the old code, a mutant or a planted bad line); the guide names the real mistake as that input. Our adaptations: the table lives in Maps/Contracts/rule-enforcers.md, not in AGENTS.md, which is at its 13,489 B ceiling; and it keeps review as an enforcer type, because blind review and Haiyuan's gates hold many of our rules today; in the guide's terms, a rule held only by review is a candidate for a higher level. Trialled now as Maps/Contracts/rule-enforcers.md (pending review): the 73 rules of AGENTS.md, numbered by line, each with its enforcer type (script, check, routine, review or policy only) and the lookup behind it; 34 are policy only, all 13 routines are Grok routines on the box, and 33 rows depend on the box, which the Mac cannot read. Status: trial idea, not installed and not scheduled: /correct is not installed, no AGENTS.md rule changes and no check is added; any install or adoption needs Haiyuan. Card requested by Haiyuan on 2026-10-20. Caveats: the guide describes its own skill and gives no measured results for it; the table's types are our reading of the files on the Mac on 2026-10-20, and its box-side rows are unverified. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: A public agent-workflow plugin guide (pstack, Oct 2026) — a per-step decision log for long or overnight runs, audited next morning by a reviewer from a different model family
entries.why: A public agent-workflow plugin guide (pstack, Oct 2026), chapter 7, 'Run work while you sleep': what makes an unattended run safe is a checkable finish condition, an isolated worktree or cloud agent, and a decision log audited in the morning. Its overnight contract carries the goal, the finish condition, permissions and an escape hatch ('if you're truly stuck after a few hours, stop and write up why'); each loop iteration is one change, one check and one log row, changes that did not help are discarded, and the finish condition never quietly relaxes. The /show-me-your-work skill records each row with the time, phase, decision, reason, an evidence pointer and the result, in a TSV at decisions.tsv (or .audit/<task-slug>.tsv when several runs share a directory); the log stays local by default and is committed when a reviewer needs the trail to trust the result. Next morning, 'catch me up on what you did last night' spawns a reviewer on a different model family to read the trail and the transcript, and the reply ends with an Attention section: read it first, then the log rows it points at, auditing decisions rather than re-reading the night. The chapter's pitfall: a duration is not a finish condition. Why it matters here: our long Mac runs stream JSON events into their run logs (AGENTS.md § Mac CLI launch; DSH has no stream-json mode), and a saved stream records each tool call the run made, but no row per decision with its reason and an evidence pointer; the morning view is the done receipt (#done-receipt) and the seat's own post-task note. The idea, our adaptation of the guide to our seats: a long or overnight Mac run keeps a decision TSV with the guide's six columns next to its run log or in its worktree; next morning a seat from a different model family than the implementer (for an Opus 5.5 run, Astra on GPT-6 Astra) reads the TSV and the saved stream, blind to the implementer's summary, and returns an Attention list that points at rows; that list feeds the done receipt's NOT VERIFIED and RISKS lines. We already have: blind review in which the implementer is never a reviewer on the same PR (#em-loop); the Nightly Mac harness audit at 02:59 PT, which rotates one Mac CLI and goes to dual LGTM; the rule that a stale run resumes only after the old agent is gone (#watchdog-resume-safety); and, as Lab cards only, overnight-receipts (a per-branch receipt built from session logs and git for the morning after unattended runs) and the Poteto x Matt Pocock interview summary (findings appended to one log and reviewed in a batch). Status: trial idea, not installed and not scheduled: no log format, wrapper, routine or review prompt changes; any install or adoption needs Haiyuan. Card requested by Haiyuan on 2026-10-20. Caveats: the guide's reviewer and Attention section are its own skill's behavior, and nothing has been measured here; a decision row is still the agent's own account, so the audit checks rows against the run log and the worktree instead of trusting them; an extra Astra read costs quota on every audited run. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: A public agent-workflow plugin guide (pstack, Oct 2026) — blind A/B evals for skill and prompt changes: the same task for both variants, candidates that do not know they are tested, one judge under neutral labels
entries.why: A public agent-workflow plugin guide (pstack, Oct 2026), chapter 9, 'Make it yours' (section 'Test a skill change blind'): a skill edit affects every future session, so it is tested like the experiment it is, and so is adopting someone else's skill: check that it makes the agent better on your work before keeping it. Ask for the eval together with the edit ('update the review skill so it flags missing migrations, and eval the change'), because a fix written from one bad session tends to overfit that session, and over many edits the skill drifts. Its Eval playbook is built around one failure mode, the observer effect: an agent that knows it is being evaluated behaves differently, so candidate agents get an organic-looking task in sanitized directories, never the words 'eval' or 'candidate', and never each other's existence; one judge scores all outputs under neutral labels; and chain-following is graded from which files each candidate actually read, not from what it claims. The user still reads every output before accepting the verdict and, on disagreeing with the judge, suspects the rubric first. The same chapter advises approving a /reflect proposal only if it would change a future decision ('One weird session is an anecdote, not a rule'), and its pitfall is editing a skill mid-task: fix it in its own PR. Why it matters here: before a skill or prompt change is promoted, our replay regression check (#replay-check) replays a few saved runs, and a replay pass means nothing broke, not that the change is good; the replay set of real failures (#replay-set) is policy text and not built; three clean runs only catch large regressions (#detection-floor); and every repeat lesson becomes a proposed skill diff (#repeat-lesson) that this test could judge. The idea, our adaptation to our seats: an A/B for a skill or prompt change, in which the old and the new text run the same task as ordinary-looking kicks in separate scratch worktrees, neither told that it is an eval or that the other exists; one judge seat scores both outputs under neutral labels (A and B); and file reading is graded from each run's saved stream-json output, whose tool-call records name the files read, not from the run's own summary. Blind dual-LGTM keeps reviewers blind to each other; this adds candidates blind to the test. We already have: the replay check inside Three-Run Proof before a skill or prompt is promoted (#replay-check, #three-run-proof); the replay set above, which came from the failure-taxonomy Lab card and is judged on the worst of three runs, in the playbook as policy text; and, as a Lab card only, Harness Wrangler (paired graded runs per task and variant, with a confidence interval on the difference and 'no headroom' when the baseline already gets it right). Status: trial idea, not installed and not scheduled: no eval harness, judge prompt or skill changes; any run spends model quota and needs Haiyuan. Card requested by Haiyuan on 2026-10-20. Caveats: the guide gives no numbers for its Eval playbook; one task per variant is anecdote-sized, so a verdict needs several tasks; our run folders (FACTS.md, review/ folders) can themselves tell a run that it is being tested, so sanitizing them is part of the trial. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: A public agent-workflow plugin guide (pstack, Oct 2026) — prove a gate, smoke or watchdog fails on a deliberately broken copy before trusting it
entries.why: A public agent-workflow plugin guide (pstack, Oct 2026), chapter 6, 'Verify and ship': its formal-verification skill 'verifies one property and shows that property failing on a broken variant of the code, because a check you've never seen fail proves nothing'; before handing over, the generator follows the new skill once on a scratch change that breaks the property, and the check must catch it; after merges and refactors, its maintain step shows that each updated check can still fail. The app-verification generator proves a new verify skill once end to end (launch, doctor check, drive one feature, capture evidence, clean up, then confirm the evidence survived the cleanup), and if that proof fails the output is not used. Chapter 9's /correct proves each new check fails on a real past mistake, and chapter 7 asks, before a loop runs unattended, that every stage proves its work and can stop the line. Why it matters here: our check-can-fail rule (#check-can-fail, 2026-10-13, policy text only) has a new check fail once on a deliberately broken input before it counts, and it is applied in places: vault bin/doc-fold-gates/ ships a --self-test that plants bad inputs in a temp copy and requires each gate to fail on every planted bad input (FAILED_TO_FAIL otherwise), to pass the untouched copy (HEALTHY_NOT_OK otherwise) and not to pass an empty input (VACUOUS otherwise), and the spawn-ok probes were tested on 2026-10-18 with a planted hang (exit 142) and a missing program (127), where a form without 'or exit 127' had exited 0, a false pass found in review (#spawn-ok). The idea: extend the rule from new checks to the standing gates, smokes and watchdogs, such as the 540 s grok-tmux-watchdog, the model-downgrade gate in grok-tmux-run (a run exits 97 when ~/bin/grok-model-check exits 3) and the model-check smoke in the daily Mac CLI update. Before one is trusted, and after each change to it, run it once on a deliberately broken copy (a dummy tmux session whose log never grows, a scratch log with a planted wrong-model event, a config copy with a planted wrong effort) and record that it fired. Reading the model gate shows why: it has caught a real downgrade (MODEL_CHECK_FAIL on #527 r1 on 10-14, per the 10-19 weekly receipts), but grok-model-check prints MODEL_CHECK_NA and exits 0 when a log holds no stream-json model events (by design, for seats without stream-json), and grok-tmux-run fails a run only on exit 3, so a coding run launched without stream-json is never failed by the model gate; a broken-copy test would surface that case. We already have: the only stall tests found in the searched notes (Maps/Decisions, Ship/builds) belong to the parked 2026-10-08 resume-safety code for the watchdog, which was never installed: a suite with fake agents in throwaway tmux sessions (~/work/lab-folds-1008/watchdog/) whose last recorded run, fix round 4, passed 246 checks; and, as Lab cards, Kanon ('a guard must be able to fail') and verified-ops-starter (44 self-test checks, each first broken by a mutant). Status: trial idea, not installed and not scheduled: no gate, watchdog or wrapper changes, and any test runs on copies in a scratch folder, never on a live run; any install or adoption needs Haiyuan. Card requested by Haiyuan on 2026-10-20. Caveats: the guide's examples are its verification skills and formal tools, so broken-copy tests for live infrastructure are our adaptation; whether the live watchdog was ever shown to fire on a stalled copy is not recorded in the notes searched, so it stays unverified. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: A public agent-workflow plugin guide (pstack, Oct 2026) — pause playbook: commit a checkpoint and write a resume note before the Mac drops or a quota ends
entries.why: A public agent-workflow plugin guide (pstack, Oct 2026), chapter 7, 'Run work while you sleep': to stop a run on purpose, the user tells the agent to pause, or that they are about to go offline or restart the app; the Pause safely playbook then finishes or backs out of the current step, commits a work-in-progress checkpoint and writes a resume note, and a fresh chat picks the work up from that note through the Session pickup playbook. Saying 'keep going' never triggers a pause. Chapter 3 describes Session pickup ('take over this branch. read the decision log, figure out what's done, and continue from there. don't redo finished work.'): it treats the prior trail as authoritative, reconstructs the branch state and decisions, names the resume point, and verifies inherited claims against the original goal instead of re-deriving everything. The guide does not list what the resume note holds; the playbook file itself is not part of the guide. Why it matters here: our runs stop for reasons nobody types. The 10-19 weekly receipts record three outages in the 10-12 to 10-19 window (Mac drops, the 10-15 exec wedge, and a stretch of silent box routines after usage ran out), and Muse hit its weekly quota on the 2026-10-20 00:34 brief, so Astra writes the brief through the 10-25 12:34 slot. Today a resume rests on the watchdog's --on-stale resume of the same session, the named session id plus a vault note (#exception-first), and ad hoc RESUME.md logs in run folders (for example ~/work/harness-1019/RESUME.md). The idea: before the Mac drops or a quota ends, or as soon as an outage is noticed, write one note from a template: the checkpoint commit in the worktree (or why there is none), the exact resume command, the tmux session, log and stream-json paths and the watchdog loop, the state of each review (seat, round, VERDICT line and SHA), what is NOT done, and the approvals pending. Our adaptations: quota ending and provider outage as triggers, the field list, and where the note goes (RESUME.md in the run folder plus a vault note). Trialled now as a template (templates/pause-resume-note.md) and a vault skill note (Agents/skills/pause-resume-note/SKILL.md), document only and not wired into any routine, wrapper or watchdog. We already have: no exit while waiting; resume only after the old agent is gone (#watchdog-resume-safety); runs an outage prevented count as skip; spawn-ok probes after Mac trouble (#spawn-ok); and, as Lab cards, CAPO (a Markdown checkpoint of git status and uncommitted changes at a quota wall, then a relaunch on the other CLI; in the playbook as a source pointer, the automatic checkpoint not built), Agent Limit Watchdog (an orderly stop: a status/handoff file, a WIP commit without push, then pause), clear-resume and context-guard (handover notes). Status: trial idea, not installed and not scheduled; the template and skill note change no routine, wrapper, watchdog or running skill; any wiring or adoption needs Haiyuan. Card requested by Haiyuan on 2026-10-20. Caveats: a sudden Mac drop leaves no turn to write the note, so whoever notices writes it from the last log, commit and kick row, marking unknowns; the checkpoint is a local commit in the run's own worktree, and pushing it stays within what the kick already allows. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: A public agent-workflow plugin guide (pstack, Oct 2026) — seven questions to answer before reporting a number
entries.why: A public agent-workflow plugin guide (pstack, Oct 2026), chapter 6, 'Verify and ship' (section 'Vet a measured number with /benchmark-checklist'): a before-and-after number is the easiest evidence to get wrong by accident, since a warm cache, a debug build on one side, or work that never ran inside the timed region can each produce a convincing speedup. The checklist asks seven questions and wants evidence from a run for each: (1) what limits the number, and why isn't it double? (2) did every side run tuned the way production runs? (3) does the result break a physical limit, like disk bandwidth or core count? (4) did anything error or return wrong output? (5) does it reproduce over alternating runs, with a median and a range? (6) does it matter end to end, on the path a user waits on? (7) did the work actually happen inside the timed region? The verdict is faster, slower, no measurable difference or inconclusive, with the run count, the range and the limiter, and it is inconclusive when the limiter cannot be named or a side ran untuned. Chapter 8 names the principle, Explain the Number: name what limits a measured number and rule out that it measured something else before anyone trusts or reports it. Why it matters here: our rules cover parts of this. A count or an all/none statement in a receipt, Decision or Lab card names how it was counted and over what (#check-can-fail); a zero needs a lookup that worked (#negative-claim-check); three clean runs only catch large regressions (#detection-floor). Several forbidden.md corrections answer question 6 after the fact (cumulative judge time is not an end-to-end speedup; a kernel speedup is not an average end-to-end agent improvement), and one is a comparison that was never timed (a video duration plus one Jev Choice latency is not a timed A/B task comparison). The idea, our adaptation, since the guide's questions are written for performance numbers: before a receipt, Decision, Lab card, usage note or brief states a number we measured ourselves (a cost, a duration, a count, a before-and-after), answer the seven questions in a line each from the run, or label the number inconclusive and say what is missing. A number quoted from a source keeps the existing caveat that it is the author's and was not re-run. Numbers of ours it would have covered: the DSH live test's 40 requests for $0.036 (10-18), worth_running's run on 139 of 142 answered calls (09-27) and the 2 stale kills in 266 watchdog marker logs (10-02 to 10-08). Status: trial idea, not installed and not scheduled: no template, receipt format or skill text changes; any adoption needs Haiyuan. Card requested by Haiyuan on 2026-10-20. Caveats: questions 2, 3, 6 and 7 assume a timed performance comparison and fit counts and costs loosely, so 'n/a: not a timing' is an allowed answer in our adaptation; the guide gives no data on how often the checklist changes a verdict. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: agent-sync: TTL task leases decided by a git-ref or atomic-file compare-and-swap
entries.why: Coordination plane for several coding agents on one repository (a standard-library-only Python 3.9+ coordinator plus four bash hooks, shipped as a skill and a plugin): leases with a TTL, race-free id reservation, a run journal, a cross-repo signal feed and a generated board. Its doctrine is two planes, 'Git is the record plane. The cloud is the coordination plane.': a fact that must survive is written to git first and only referenced from the cloud, while who is doing what right now lives in the cloud and expires. The load-bearing measurement is the author's: 'twelve concurrent appends to one document returned twelve successes and left three lines', so 'The knowledge base never decides a lease.' Exclusion comes only from a primitive with a real compare-and-swap: an atomic file create (the local backend, exclusive on one machine, advisory across machines) or a pushed git ref (the git backend, where the remote's non-fast-forward rejection is the compare-and-swap); status, acquire and check all state which guarantee you have, 'because a lease that is not actually exclusive is worse than none: the other agent has stopped checking.' Defaults: a 2,700-second TTL, renewed every 300 seconds by a post-tool-use hook; acquire prints won or lost <holder>, and release reports NOT released (exit 1) until the remote no longer has the ref. 'A lease is a promise to come back': an abandoned one blocks its task until the TTL, and the next agent cannot tell in progress from crashed an hour ago. The lease (who holds the task now) is kept apart from the durable claim, a git tag naming the run, written through on acquire and restored verbatim on release: one fact, one home. status lists the other runs' live holdings and new signals, watermarked per run; ids are allocated positionally over the log, so two agents cannot be handed one number, and timestamps only expire a lease. A pre-tool-use guard denies an edit or commit to a guarded register without a live lease, parsing shell writes (redirects, tee, sed -i, cp, mv, git add then commit) in the repository that owns each target. Stated limits: the hooks bind on one coding CLI only, so on other agents a run is a self-check recorded ungated; its fs option is not cross-machine; and sweeping old leases by age is the operator's decision, never an agent's. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, several Mac CLI seats and the always-on bots work against one vault and often one checkout, so the collision surface is two seats editing the same register, the same Lab entries or the same roadmap row. The pack places it beside kept dibs (2026-10-03), which holds the single-machine lease lane but is reference-only, has no SPDX licence and is Rust plus SQLite on one machine; the delta is the guarantee ladder (local mutex against git compare-and-swap, stated in the same words), TTL plus renew, run-named claim tags, per-run signal watermarks and id reservation, and the twelve-appends result is the citable sentence: a knowledge base cannot arbitrate a lease, however many agents agree to read it. We already have: six Mac CLI seats (#roster) and one shared vault that every bot and Mac CLI reads before work and files to after it (#vault); exclusive ownership of a run's output listed as proposed in the controls inventory, with the old process checked by hand before a resume today and an ownership guard (attempt IDs; no restart unless the old process is proven dead) staged, not installed (#controls-inventory); a resume only after the old agent is confirmed gone, since a resume beside a surviving one leaves two agents acting on one worktree (#watchdog-resume-safety); the 10-15 lesson in which two seats held the same pack path for about 3 minutes (#mac-run-lessons); and the #10 review precedent, whose recurring findings were one multi-writer race class (shared state with no fencing or ownership token), with one owner or epoch token per record as the named redesign (#leftover-p2). Per the pack, nothing in the fleet installer or the EM loop takes a lease today, and dibs was never applied. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): a scratch-repo trial on the git backend in which two seats acquire one key, the loser must see lost <holder>, and one register file is guarded; exclusion only on a compare-and-swap primitive (atomic file create or git ref), each lease stating its guarantee, and release on failure as the default. On the pinned harness seat it would load as a plain skill but stay advisory (ungated) until a hook exists. The pack's stop condition: if the git compare-and-swap is slow or unreliable on our remote, fall back to the local backend and label it advisory, never implying exclusion. Leases on live repos, the vault or the Lab entries would be a separate Haiyuan decision. Caveats: the twelve-appends measurement and the defaults are the author's, read in the README, not re-run; enforcement binds on one coding CLI only and the local backend on one machine only, so elsewhere a lease is a self-check; MIT, 4 stars, created 2026-07-29, pushed 2026-10-20; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: pctl: tmux control plane that reports what happened to a message typed into a pane
entries.why: tmux-based control plane for interactive coding-agent sessions (Rust 1.99 or newer, tmux 3.8 or newer; macOS arm64 and Linux): one tmux server per state directory, sessions addressed by name, and commands to list, read, prompt, wait on a session, restart it on the same conversation and restore it after a reboot. Session state is named, not inferred: idle, working, waits for you, exited, stopped. The part the pack would take is pctl tell <to> <text>: it sends to a session here, to <machine>:<name> on another computer, to an agent over an agent-to-agent protocol or to another coding CLI's session by prefix, prefixes [from <me> <host> <cwd>], and then reports what happened: reached, queued behind the target's work, typed_unconfirmed, queued_typing (a person is typing) or queued_blocked (a human decision is pending), each exit 0. A detected mix stays unsubmitted (mixed_draft, exit 5) for the person to review; it never pretends a keystroke landed. Worktree workers: session add --worktree <branch> creates the branch and a <repo>-wt-<name> worktree, worktree list shows branch, base, dirty files, commits ahead and whether merged, and worktree remove moves only a stopped, clean, merged worktree to the trash and refuses anything else. The web page answers only on loopback or tailnet addresses, keeps its token file at mode 0600 and refuses input to blocked sessions; Markdown is inert on the main origin, and HTML, SVG and PDF go through an isolated service. Its own boundary: 'It is not a sandbox: the state directory is trusted local state.' The README calls it private and under active development, with no CI and no auto-merge; pull requests paste exact commands and results, and the maintainer re-runs them. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our tmux and watchdog lane is deep, but its kept cards (tmux-agent-status, gate-inbox, @juli-os/agents, agent-perch) cover session state or restart policy, not a named delivery outcome for a message typed into another seat's pane. Per the pack, our launch and watchdog path types into panes and assumes it worked; pctl names five delivery outcomes and refuses to submit a mixed draft, the rule the pack says our handoff packets need. The pack also reads restart on the same conversation as the resume semantics a watchdog should aim at, and the not-a-sandbox sentence as one that belongs verbatim in the launch skill. We already have: every long Mac CLI run launched through a tmux wrapper with streaming output and a stale-log watchdog (~540 s) whose on-stale action resumes the same session, each tool's session id reused per PR or slice (#launch); a resume only after the old agent is confirmed gone, checked by hand, with a run whose old agent survives or cannot be read parked as an unknown outcome (#watchdog-resume-safety); the 10-15 lesson in which the watchdog re-ran an idle catch-up collect cold twice, a new conversation each time, before the agent's own 15-minute background wait could end (#mac-run-lessons); spawn-ok probes after any Mac trouble, one of them a timed tmux -V (#spawn-ok); a coding kick ledger whose rows move posted → launched → pr_open or done, or blocked with a note, and a named unacked-handoff failure mode, a room-only kick the heartbeat never read (#coding-em-kicks); a machine-readable handoff packet (from, to, job_type, objective, artifacts, decisions, constraints, open questions, next gate) that carries the work's state, not a delivery outcome (#handoff-packet); and the rule that the stale-only watchdog is not fleet-replaced without Haiyuan's ask (#exception-first). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the five delivery states (reached, queued, typed_unconfirmed, queued_typing, queued_blocked) and the mixed_draft refusal written into our tmux wrapper's logs now, with nothing installed, so a typed message is never taken as evidence of delivery; restart on the same conversation as the target for watchdog resumes; and the not-a-sandbox sentence carried verbatim into the launch skill. The pack's stop condition: any trial that types into a pane without a delivery verdict is not a trial. Installing pctl waits for tmux 3.8 or newer and a disposable state directory; the tmux upgrade, any wrapper or watchdog change and any install would each need Haiyuan. Caveats: this Mac has tmux 3.7c (the pack's spawn-ok probe, 2026-10-20), while pctl requires 3.8 or newer and calls older versions untested, so a trial needs a tmux upgrade first; the delivery vocabulary is the author's and has not been tried against our seats; by its own statement it is not a sandbox; private, under active development and without CI; MIT, 0 stars, created 2026-10-16, pushed 2026-10-20; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: session-counter: recounts retry give-ups, watchdog kills and lost agents from local logs
entries.why: Recounts four kinds of failure from the session logs a coding CLI already writes locally, using two counters, one in Node and one in Python, each standard library only (no install, no network, no dependencies); per the README both print the same bytes and pass 12 of 12 fixtures each, including a test that every fixture file is byte-for-byte unchanged after a run. (1) Failed API requests, chained through parentUuid into incidents: an incident is one request that failed and was retried, and its outcome is the first assistant record after the chain (recovered, gave up or unknown); repeats are counted once and reported separately. (2) Retry give-ups: incidents that ended with the client giving up. (3) Watchdog kills: an agent attempt whose last record is the interrupt marker written 175 seconds or more after the previous record, the workflow watchdog stopping an agent that made no progress for about 180 s; a sooner marker is a short stop, not counted. (4) Agents lost or never reported back, grouped by the reason the final run record gives, plus runs still marked completed although they hold a lost agent (2 in the sample). The output holds counts only, never a path, an id or any log text, so it can be pasted into a report without sharing logs. The author's one real check, on their own 1–3 Oct logs: 208 failed requests in 54 incidents (47 recovered, 7 give-ups), 353 watchdog kills (323 restarted, 17 short stops) and 39 lost agents. Stated cannots: not why a request failed; a watchdog kill is only about 180 s without model progress, so a slow first token, a hung connection and a queued server look alike; failed requests inside workflow agents are not counted; the totals do not add up on purpose, since the classes overlap; the log layout is undocumented and may change; retention may have deleted older logs. It rates itself version 0.1.0 at the TOOL rung: 'next rung needs: a review and one real run by someone other than the maker.' Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our usage and routine-fire lane counts scheduler fires, not what happened inside the run, and this asks a different question: did the harness lose work? Per the pack, retry give-ups, watchdog kills, lost agents and never-reported agents are what our catch-up kicks and green-run dashboards cannot see, the runs-still-marked-completed count is a direct measure of false green in our own fleet, and 'totals do not add up on purpose' is the right shape for a dashboard that must not invent a single score. The pack sets it beside kept overnight-receipts (a per-branch PASSED, UNVERIFIED or FAILED receipt) and a kept drift-alert card, which ask other questions. We already have: a public usage dashboard refreshed three times daily (#controls-inventory), whose routine fire proxy is coarse cron fires per week labeled PROXY, beside per-seat quota and health cards (#usage); one receipt line per routine run (ok, skip, fail or parked), written even when nothing happened (#receipt-line); a completion claim that counts only when the session record backs it (#claim-vs-record), done decided by a deterministic check with self-reports advisory (#code-decides-done), and a NOT VERIFIED line never omitted from a done receipt (#done-receipt); a count that names how it was counted and over what (#check-can-fail); a hand count of stale kills, 2 of 266 watchdog marker logs from 2026-10-02 to 10-08 (#watchdog-resume-safety); the 10-15 lesson in which each cold re-run of an idle catch-up collect ended with a SUCCESS result and no pack (#mac-run-lessons), the false-green shape this tool counts; report-only checks that read state and write a report but never kill, block or edit, installed with no schedule (#report-only-checks); and weekly receipts, because a bot can summarize its history but should not be its only judge (#kill-review). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): a read-only run on one seat's log root for a fixed 7-day window, compared with the usage dashboard's fires; the four classes kept separate in any report, with no single score; and the runs-still-marked-completed count read as a false-green measure next to our receipt lines. The pack's stop condition: no promotion until a second person runs it, by the tool's own rung rule. A schedule, a dashboard card or using its counts as a gate would be a separate Haiyuan decision. Caveats: it reads one coding CLI's local logs, in a layout the author calls undocumented and liable to change, so a trial covers only a seat whose CLI writes that layout, and retention may already have removed older logs; its watchdog class is a ~180 s no-progress marker in that log, a different clock from our ~540 s stale-log watchdog (#launch), so how our kills would show up is unverified; the 1–3 Oct counts and fixture results are the author's, read in the README, not re-run, and none is ours; MIT for code and Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 for text, 0 stars, created 2026-10-06, pushed 2026-10-19; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: Remote agent worker: remote box runs the agent loop; the hub pulls only final artifacts
entries.why: Host plugin for the coding-agent harness one of our seats runs (no third-party dependencies; Node ^22.19 or 24 and newer) that turns another computer into a remote worker. The hub keeps the model, credentials and session logs; the worker runs its own copy of the harness and an independent agent loop, and the task persists there. The hub receives a handoff result card and an artifact manifest, and finished files cross only on an explicit remote_pull. Two task modes: exec (default approval manual, so it waits for a human; 10-minute timeout) and agent (the worker starts its own session; 1-hour timeout; model picked from the worker's advertised list, and headless backends that cannot take a model are refused before dispatch). Stated invariants: credentials never leave the worker; a disconnect does not terminate the task; the relay sees ciphertext only (X25519 and AES-256-GCM); manifest before bytes; only role:final artifacts cross; and a resumable pull keeps received bytes and resumes with startOffset and prefixSha256, checked by a whole-file SHA-256. On reconnect, task/sync reconciles and completed tasks do not rerun. Four read-only file tools (remote_ls/read/grep/tree) ride a separate frame and take no queue place or concurrency slot, so they answer while the worker is busy. Write guards: confirm: 'yes', no overwrite by default, no recursive delete, atomic writes, an 8 MB cap, target and parent inside the configured roots, symlinks listed but not dereferenced; remote_kill refuses the plugin's own process, its parent and system-critical processes. Config patching edits a managed block only, with a timestamped backup, re-parse, duplicate-id check, rollback and one-click undo, and never uses 0.0.0.0, which new host versions hard-reject (the README cites 10 crash logs). A doctor runs 8 checks, each with its fix, and tells never connected from connected then dropped. The author reports 987 tests (985 pass, 2 skip) and 123 doc-drift assertions, the host verified at 0.2.0-rc.2, full validation on Windows, and macOS and Linux covered by CI. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, this is the box-to-Mac staging surface, and the Mac-offline class is why today's pack exists: it is the catch-up of a 09:00 PT kick that fired while the Mac was offline (outage from about 07:37 PT, gap: MISS_MAC). Per the pack, kept handoff cards (sctxx, Context Guard, clear-resume, relevo) move state between contexts, and none moves execution to a machine that stays up. The transferable shape, per the pack: the missing run is not lost but queued on the worker, on reconnect task/sync reconciles and completed tasks do not rerun, and only final artifacts cross, the guarantee a catch-up kick wants. We already have: that seat pinned to the 0.2.1 line (0.2.1-rc.2 or newer, never back to 0.2.0), manual-update-only, with a 0.2.0-rc.2 rollback tarball kept (#providers), on the hourly collect rotation and an optional implementer (#roster), the pin marked enforced though a manual downgrade is not blocked (#controls-inventory); the Mac vault path as source of truth, with work staged on the box, marked STAGED ON BOX and copied once the Mac is up (playbook §12, box↔Mac vault sync); two collect seats that can write only inside their own workspace, so the bot that publishes the brief copies their packs to packs/ (#field-brief-12h); spawn-ok probes after any Mac trouble, and if one fails nothing is launched or resumed and a gap is recorded (#spawn-ok); unknown outcomes after a crash or dirty exit parked, not auto-retried (#retry-ceiling); runs an outage prevented counted as skip, not fail, with the outage and what was caught up recorded once (#kill-condition); another agent's output treated as data, never instructions (#untrusted-content); and permissions and production on the RED list, with anything that cannot be undone in under a minute parked for Haiyuan (#gyr-authority). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the pattern first, run the loop where the work is, so a hub restart reconciles instead of rerunning, only final artifacts cross and credentials stay on the worker; then a trial on our pinned 0.2.1 build on macOS with scratch roots, manual approval and no relay or SMB, whose acceptance test is to kill the hub mid-task, restart it and show the completed task is not rerun. The pack's kill condition: the version mismatch (0.2.0-rc.2 tested against our 0.2.1 pin) or any remote-write surprise kills the trial. Installing a host plugin with remote write and kill powers would be a separate Haiyuan decision. Caveats: the author verified 0.2.0-rc.2 while our pin is the 0.2.1 line, and the pin rules out going back to 0.2.0 to match, so a trial would itself be the 0.2.1 test; full validation is Windows and macOS is CI-only, while our seats run on the Mac; it installs a host plugin with remote write and kill powers; nodeToken is unchecked by default and the transport has no TLS; the test counts and the 10 crash logs are the author's, read in the README, not re-run; MIT, 2 stars, created 2026-10-13, pushed 2026-10-20; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: vault-memory: local recall index that ranks stale notes down and flags contradictions
entries.why: Standard-library Python 3.9+ tool (a skill, a local tool server and a CLI; nothing leaves the machine) that turns a notes vault into memory any agent can ask: a local index, a frontmatter contract, a link graph, freshness tracking and a synthesis of what repeats, all deterministic, with no network, no model and zero tokens. recall searches by text, by id (order, case or record) and by ticket key, returns the exact paragraph rather than the whole file, and refreshes itself when the vault changed. Freshness: replaced, expired and unverified notes rank lower, and two current notes about the same fact are reported as a contradiction. Safe writing: note validates the contract and refuses duplicates, making you update or replace instead; doctor says how much frontmatter is missing, and fix fills it without overwriting anything or moving files. The graph shows backlinks, orphan notes, broken wikilinks and duplicate names; patterns show what repeats, what repeats without a written solution and what has been open too long. usage answers whether memory is helping (pointers used, missed recall, gaps), eval measures recall against your own questions, and a curate skill turns doctor plus usage into a short weekly list of what to merge, close or stop suggesting. The panel is a self-contained HTML page that embeds note titles and excerpts, explicitly local-only and never to be published; index, telemetry and panel live in the vault's state folder. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, the vault is our primary durable memory, yet every pack still dedupes by hand: grep the 186 Lab entries, grep the last packs, remember the folds (today the box-side seen-links file was not readable from the Mac either, so the curate must still apply that skip list). Per the pack, kept Agentic Vault Skeleton covers layout (one rules file, an off-limits map, a bounded session cache) and the kept memory-loop card covers write discipline, but neither covers the read path; the delta is recall quality measured, not asserted: freshness ranking, contradiction pairs, repeats without a written solution, and usage and eval that say whether pointers were used or missed. The pack also reads the contradiction rule as the right guard for a vault where two notes can both look current. We already have: a shared vault on the Mac as the team's long-term memory, a context repo rather than a chat log (#vault); recall that greps the notes' one-line summary lines and opens in full only the notes that apply, summaries written with the exact names a later search would use, a start-of-task line naming the notes used or saying nothing applies, and a missed recall fixed in the summary line or the search, not the lesson (#memory-loop); consolidation that merges lessons saying the same thing and deletes durable lessons only after Haiyuan approves each item on a prune list, policy text that nothing enforces (#memory-loop); a provenance card (claim, source, owner, status, supersedes, review_after) on each Decision note and standing-rule memory, new notes only (#memory-rules); cited vault paths that must resolve, also checked over AGENTS.md and the role cards in the Monday card sync, with the lint tool not installed (#pointer-check); the repeat-lesson rule, prompted by 18 near-identical paragraphs in the never-again list, that turns a correction already filed twice into a proposed fix where the rule is applied (#repeat-lesson); source conflicts settled by the newest dated source, an open one written as TBD (conflict), in the sweep before a fold's review (#review-round-breaker); and the shared-memory admission rules, untouched here (#shared-memory-admission). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): read-only recall and doctor on a copy of the vault first, with missed recall measured against this pack's hand dedupe, under the pack's playbook line: ask the vault, measure recall, rank stale notes down, report contradictions and retire what the code absorbed. The pack's stop conditions: no fix --apply without a backup, and publishing the panel is forbidden because it embeds excerpts. The pack names the frontmatter standard as the real adoption cost; a frontmatter contract across the vault, or the tool writing to the live vault, would be a separate Haiyuan decision. Caveats: 0 stars, created and pushed 2026-10-20; index, telemetry and panel are written inside the vault's state folder, so even a read-only trial belongs on a copy; our deletes of durable lessons stay item by item with Haiyuan's approval, so its curate list could only feed a prune list (#memory-loop); the panel embeds note titles and excerpts and must never reach the public hub; its recall, usage and eval measures are the author's design, and nothing has been measured here; MIT; README-verified only, not installed or run.
