Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: agent-orchestra: only an independent verifier's witnessed PASS can mark a task done
entries.why: Governed coordination protocol for multi-agent work (zero dependencies, Node 18 or newer) built on one invariant: 'Agents can work. They cannot declare success.' The README names the failure it removes, 'an agent says it is done, and nothing in the system is able to disagree', and removes it 'by making the interesting rules checks in code rather than requests in a prompt.' Eight contracts are defined in AGENT-ORCHESTRA-PROTOCOL.md (Task, Resource, Ownership, Handoff, Verification, Evidence, Approval, Recovery), and CONFORMANCE.md pins 41 requirements (38 ENFORCED, 1 DOCUMENTED ONLY, 2 OUT OF SCOPE), each with a machine-checked test reference. The load-bearing mechanisms: one primary writer per file or resource, reviewers restricted to isolated artifacts, and a conflicting claim refused with holder and task name; an independent verification gate, where an author's self-check is never a verification result, the verifier is chosen by capability score with the implementer excluded, and the gate fails closed when no eligible verifier exists; a recorded witness artifact for every verification PASS; a graded evidence ladder from E1 (a reproducible command plus its output) to E4 (planned), so self-assertion cannot pose as evidence; and a ceiling on failure: a task blocks after 3 failed verification rounds and cannot reach done or deploy without a human override that records approver, scope and reason. The author's benchmark (bench/protocol-benchmark.mjs; scripted deterministic actors, no model calls) compares a single agent, a naive multi-agent setup and Agent Orchestra on six failure modes: conflicting resource writes, done declared with no evidence, an implementer verifying its own work, a deploy attempted without approval and a success claim after a failure each score 1, 1 and 0, and a runaway verification loop 25, 25 and at most 3 attempts; the author also reports 106 engine, 8 acceptance and 8 handoff tests, 83 activation cases and 12 injected-fault tests in scripts/gate.mjs. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, it operationalizes three of Haiyuan's standing rules, code decides done, disproof framing with blind review, and the three-fix ceiling before escalation, as an executable state machine with a reproducible fault benchmark, where our EM loop holds the policy in Markdown decisions. Per the pack, kept agent-role-contracts (2026-10-19) catches stale handoffs and self-review before execution, while this enforces the execution-to-completion gate in code. We already have: done only when a concrete, deterministic check passes, with agent self-reports advisory (#code-decides-done); a completion claim that counts only when the session record backs it, and a green run after a weakened test treated as SUSPECT, a prose rule with no hook installed (#claim-vs-record); a new check run once against a deliberately broken input and seen to fail before it counts (#check-can-fail); done receipts whose VERIFIED line lists only checks that actually ran, each with evidence, and whose NOT VERIFIED line is never omitted (#done-receipt); blind reviewers who name 2–3 rejection criteria before reading the diff, a FAIL returning evidence and a PASS listing what was tried (#disproof-review); an EM loop in which the agent that wrote the code cannot approve it (#em-loop); a cap of three fix or correction rounds, then escalation to Haiyuan (#retry-ceiling); and, in the controls inventory, one agent per run or worktree enforced by the ownership guard since 2026-10-20 (attempt IDs; only the current attempt can publish), while completion validation and the fix-round bounds stay manual, rounds counted by hand with no enforcing wrapper live (#controls-inventory). Per the pack, our EM loop relies on reviewer prompts and manual checks, and no automated fault gate or E1–E4 evidence grader is wired in. What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): a scratch-repo trial that runs bench/protocol-benchmark.mjs against a scratch task to confirm that no self-declaration is accepted, plus a trial of the 3-attempt ceiling; then the 12-fault gate wired into our test suite as an advisory pre-merge check; and the pack's playbook line: agents can work, they cannot declare success: enforce independent verification by capability score, require a witness artifact for every PASS, and block execution after 3 failed rounds. The pack's stop condition: the benchmark actors need external dependencies or fail to run deterministically on Node 18 or newer. Wiring it into a live repo's CI or the EM loop, letting it block a merge, or letting a capability score pick the verifier where our reviewer seats are fixed by rule (#reviewer-rule) would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. Caveats: the benchmark scores, the test counts and the 41-requirement conformance table are the author's, read in the README, not re-run, and none is ours; the benchmark's actors are scripted and make no model calls, so it shows what the rules refuse, not how live agents behave under them; 3 of the 41 requirements are not marked enforced (1 documented only, 2 out of scope); the pack records no check of this Mac's Node version; Apache-2.0, 99 stars, created 2026-10-19, pushed 2026-10-21; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: agent-handoff-mcp: handoffs as append-only queued → accepted → completed records
entries.why: Local-first tool server (Node.js 22.13 or newer, TypeScript; Streamable HTTP and stdio transports; SQLite in WAL mode with parameterized queries) that gives several agents a shared inbox without giving one model control over another. Per the README, multi-agent systems often pass work through unstructured chat transcripts or ad hoc files and lose ownership, lifecycle state, authorization boundaries and audit trails; here a handoff is a protocol object that moves sender → queued → accepted → completed, or queued → blocked → completed, and the sender may cancel only while it is queued. Its boundary: the server coordinates work and explicitly does not execute agents, fetch references, read arbitrary files or create autonomous agent loops; references are stored as inert strings and never dereferenced. Six tools: handoff_whoami (identity, boundaries, policy revision), handoff_send (to an authorized recipient), handoff_inbox (the tasks for an identity), handoff_get (a task and its append-only event history), handoff_acknowledge (accept queued or blocked work) and handoff_update_status (mark blocked or completed, or cancel while queued). Stated security invariants: explicit send_to and receive_from authorization with no permissive defaults; a disclosure ceiling per agent (public-safe, internal, restricted); append-only lifecycle events, with no delete tool; a maximum reply-chain depth against automated ping-pong loops; token bindings with SHA-256 digests; and immutable policy snapshots, so a revocation takes effect on live sessions without a restart. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, we coordinate the always-on bots, Mac CLI seats and subagents across separate contexts, and today a receiver can drop a task or miss an acknowledgment. Per the pack, kept pctl (2026-10-20) covers delivery into a tmux pane and kept handoff-bus (2026-10-19) provides named lines, while this adds the standard protocol layer for cross-seat handoffs with an append-only SQLite audit ledger; the pack also reads its inert-references invariant as direct support for our untrusted-content rule. We already have: a machine-readable handoff packet on every Manage → specialist handoff and every new coding kick row (from, to, job_type, objective, artifacts, decisions, constraints, open_questions, next_gate), so ownership passes, not transcripts, with its completeness check run in shadow only, never blocking (#handoff-packet); a coding kick ledger whose rows move posted → launched → pr_open or done, or blocked with a note, read first by the EM bot's */15 heartbeat, where a kick posted with no seat is launched or marked blocked, never left idle, and a named unacked-handoff failure mode, a room-only kick the heartbeat never read (#coding-em-kicks); written handoff contracts in which every actionable Manage → specialist message carries goal, owner, trigger, artifact path, verified, assumptions, waiting-approval, open questions and return shape (playbook §12, written handoff contracts); in group rooms, only the first @mention in a bot reply waking another bot, a hop cap of 2 (1 in the Field Brief room after a miss ticket) before asking Haiyuan, and at most one ack and one final per task (playbook §12, group rooms); and another agent's output treated as data, never instructions, any instructions in it quoted to Haiyuan, as policy text that nothing enforces (#untrusted-content). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): a two-seat trial over the stdio transport between two local CLI test sessions that checks the sender can cancel only while a task is queued, that references stay inert and that the reply-depth bound holds; and the pack's playbook line: handoffs are protocol objects, not chat transcripts: keep an append-only state machine (queued → accepted → completed), allow cancel only while queued, and treat references as inert strings. The pack's kill condition: any attempt by the server to dereference paths or execute commands on its own kills the trial. Using it for live handoffs, beside or in place of the kick ledger and the packets, or giving a live seat its tools would be a separate Haiyuan decision. Caveats: the lifecycle, the tool list and the invariants are the author's, read in the README, and none was tested here; the pack's trial uses the stdio transport, not Streamable HTTP; the pack records no check of this Mac's Node version against 22.13; Apache-2.0, 2 stars, created 2026-10-16, pushed 2026-10-21; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: conspectus: read-only, evidence-ranked map of agent sessions, tmux panes and worktrees
entries.why: Rust CLI and library (version 0.1.0, a pre-release; a zero-copy snapshot format and an XDG cache layout) that builds one provider-neutral map of the agent work on a machine: it locates agent sessions across multiple CLIs, terminal multiplexers (tmux, zellij), git repositories, worktrees, branches and forge pull requests, records plausible relationships as evidence and resolves them into a typed graph of 10 node kinds (agent session, mux session, repo, checkout, branch, workspace, fork, forge PR, pin, runtime process) and 22 typed relations. The graph is sparse by default: an orphan session or an unlinked tmux pane is valid data, never an error. Evidence first, resolution second: discovery never guesses; a plausible relationship is a candidate link with provenance (declared, strongly discovered, discovered, convention, cached), a confidence score and freshness, and resolvers select the preferred link while keeping the losing candidates, so an ambiguity stays visible as data (a ⚠ glyph and score breakdowns) instead of collapsing silently. Attribution follows six ranks without touching the agents: (1) a link declared in configuration; (2) a session the harness reported, or a pane process with the transcript open (/proc, lsof); (3) the harness's internal state or logs, read-only; (4) the harness process running in the pane, found by a process-tree walk; (5) the pane's launch command (argv) naming the session; (6) the pane's working directory matching the session. Pins are sessions that outlive processes: logical sessions declared by name and directory, whose compaction, resume and crash lineage is tracked so that a single command reconnects to the latest active conversation rather than spawning a fresh, disjoint session. Bounded mutation envelope: strictly read-only by default; it never types into a live agent pane and never writes harness-owned state. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our Mac fleet runs several long-running sessions across tmux panes, and tracking which pane runs which conversation, branch or task takes a manual grep. Per the pack, kept pctl covers message delivery while this covers session-to-multiplexer-to-git attribution, and its attribution rule (never type into a live pane to ask for a session id; walk the process tree and inspect open file descriptors) and its pins that outlive processes across compaction solve session tracking without intrusive instrumentation; the pack counts it, with pctl and agent-perch, as holding the tmux and session-viewer lane. We already have: every long Mac CLI run launched through a tmux wrapper with streaming output and a stale-log watchdog (~540 s) whose on-stale action resumes the same session, each tool's session id reused per PR or slice (#launch); the rule that a stale run resumes only after the old agent's process is confirmed gone, because killing a stale tmux session does not prove the old agent stopped, enforced since 2026-10-20 12:16 PT by the ownership guard: each launch gets an attempt ID and a workspace, a restart is refused unless the old process is proven dead, and a session launched before the install has no ownership record, so on a stall it is parked, never killed (#watchdog-resume-safety); in the same entry, tmux-agent-status's lsof-to-rollout matching for one coding CLI listed as not adopted (#watchdog-resume-safety); the EM bot's */15 heartbeat, which reads the kick ledger before inventorying tmux and PRs (#em-loop), and an 08:06 PT pickup check that cross-checks the ledger against tmux and PRs (#coding-em-kicks); the 10-11 lesson in which a run's tmux session vanished while its agent kept running, so the queue's loop ended and the stall was found by a manual check, and the 10-15 lesson in which the watchdog re-ran an idle catch-up collect cold twice, a new conversation each time (#mac-run-lessons); and report-only checks that read state and write a report but never kill, block, restart or edit anything, installed with no schedule (#report-only-checks). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): a read-only run of its graph generation on local repository checkouts that tests process-tree attribution without typing into any pane; then the six-rank attribution model and the pin lineage logic carried into our tmux status checks; and the pack's playbook line: attribute sessions by evidence, not by typing into panes: resolve process trees and open file descriptors, keep ambiguities visible as data, and track session lineage across restarts. The pack's stop condition: attribution relies on typing into panes or fails to tell concurrent tmux sessions apart. Its open-file rank would revisit the lsof matching the playbook lists as not adopted; adopting that rank, scheduling the tool, or using its graph in a resume decision would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. Caveats: version 0.1.0 is a pre-release; the six ranks, the node kinds and the provenance classes are the author's design and have not been tried against our seats or their session files; MIT, 0 stars, created 2026-08-01, pushed 2026-10-21; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: Command-silence watchdog: warns on 90 s of output silence, not on total run time
entries.why: Command watchdog, a Node.js extension for one coding agent, that warns when a command stops producing output, with silence as the primary detection signal. Its doctrine, per the README: the host agent's bash tool has no default timeout and judges success only by exit code, so the worst case, a process that is alive but already broken, never produces a failure signal; 90 seconds of silence is a real signal, while a command having run for 90 seconds is not. Streaming awareness against wall-clock duration: while output keeps flowing (a 6-minute build that logs continuously, for example) it never warns; tools that do not stream (read, write, grep, ls) use wall-clock thresholds, 180 s for a warning and 600 s for critical; known-slow commands such as docker build or cargo build raise the thresholds to 300 s and 600 s; interactive commands (vim, less, git rebase -i) are skipped entirely; and while the agent waits on human input (a permission dialog, a selector) the clock freezes, so the wait is not treated as a hang. Safe by construction: the default is pure observation (mode observe), and it never kills a process or aborts a turn without an explicit opt-in (guard or yolo); it never overrides built-in tools, never rewrites commands and never modifies tool input. The author reports 82 test cases plus a live check of RPC event order. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, its silence rule would let our watchdogs trigger earlier on genuine hangs (90 s of silence, for example) while legitimate 10-minute compilation jobs still finish undisturbed. We already have: a stale-log watchdog (~540 s) attached to every long Mac CLI run, with streaming output required and an on-stale action that resumes the same session (#launch); in the controls inventory, a log silent past 540 s with no watchdog STALE action counted as a fail, and the launch standard itself a convention that nothing blocks (#controls-inventory); an EM heartbeat every 15 minutes across live agent tasks (stretched from every 5 minutes on 2026-09-21), which does not replace the ~540 s watchdog, since both apply (#em-loop); named long-CLI failure modes (crash, hang, stall, api-error), each to leave a machine-readable heartbeat that says whether the run finished and what killed it, with loop patterns kept distinct from the stale-only watchdog and that watchdog not fleet-replaced without Haiyuan's ask (#exception-first); the 10-15 lesson in which the watchdog's on-stale action re-ran a catch-up collect cold twice while the collect sat idle waiting up to 15 minutes on a background task, each run ending with a SUCCESS result and no pack, and the 10-11 lesson in which a tracing plugin's pre- and post-tool-use hooks hung 1.5–6+ minutes per tool call and stalled two runs (#mac-run-lessons); and a count of stale kills, 2 of 266 watchdog marker logs from 2026-10-02 to 10-08 (#watchdog-resume-safety). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): its 90 s silence rule carried into our watchdog's logic, observe mode first, and evaluated on slow compilation tasks; and the pack's playbook line: silence is the watchdog signal, not elapsed runtime: warn when streaming output freezes for 90 seconds, but never interrupt a long job that is actively logging. Our watchdog's trigger is already silence, a run log silent past 540 s (#controls-inventory), so the new parts would be three proposed improvements, none approved: (1) command-level observation, with silence measured on each command's own output, not only on the run's log as a whole; (2) a pause for human input distinguished from a hang on stdin: the extension skips interactive commands and freezes its clock while the agent waits on a permission dialog or selector, and the pack's example of a genuine hang is a process that hung on stdin 10 seconds into a turn; and (3) the threshold evaluated, 90 s of silence against our ~540 s, on those slow compilation tasks. The pack's stop condition: false alerts fire during continuous streaming output. Any change to the watchdog's logic, thresholds or on-stale action would be a separate Haiyuan decision. Caveats: it is an extension for a coding agent that is not one of our seats (#roster), so what could transfer is the rule, not the extension; its thresholds are the author's defaults, not tuned on our runs; the 82 test cases and the event-order check are the author's, read in the README, not re-run; MIT, 2 stars, created and pushed 2026-10-16; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: trace: temporal-logic monitors over tool-call sequences, plus a signed audit certificate
entries.why: Interpretable, CPU-only runtime guardrail (Python 3.9 or newer; Tsetlin logic plus finite-trace linear temporal logic, LTL) that wraps an agent's tool calls and emits a cryptographic session certificate that can be verified independently. Its finding: memoryless per-call filters fail on multi-step temporal attacks; in slow-roll exfiltration every individual export call looks benign while the sequence violates policy (count_le(export, 2, 50)), and the author reports an attack success rate of 1.000 for per-call filters against 0.000 for TRACE, with false-positive rates of 0.048 or less. Three components: (1) a content guard, a Tsetlin machine that flags prompt injection and jailbreaks with human-readable Boolean clauses (IF ignore AND previous → UNSAFE), running in about 107 µs; (2) a behaviour guard, online, bounded-memory finite-trace LTL monitors (Always, Never, BoundedCount, Response, Precedence) that evaluate temporal policies at O(1) per step (4.9 µs / 322 B); (3) a certificate ledger, a hash-chained, HMAC-signed, Merkle-rooted audit log that an external party re-verifies offline without calling a model. It normalizes tool calls from multiple frontier providers into one canonical schema. Documented limitation: F1 of 0.827–0.967 in distribution collapsed to 0.209 under cross-dataset shift, taken as evidence that static syntactic rules need temporal and behavioural anchoring. The author reports 40 passing unit tests. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our harness contracts set strict policies (no secrets in notes, read-before-write, the three-round fix ceiling, human approval before external action), and compliance is checked today by post-hoc reviews or prompt instructions. Per the pack, TRACE is a lightweight formal monitor (4.9 µs, CPU-only) for multi-step sequence invariants, such as the pack's examples precedence("authorize", "deploy") and bounded_count("retry", 3, window=10), that outputs a verifiable certificate, and it shows that safety constraints can be deterministic and mathematically verified without adding model latency. We already have: run limits that long fires inherit (50 items, 2 retries, $0 spend, 0 external actions without Haiyuan's approval) and a stop on abnormal input volume, as policy in charters and skills, with a wrapper that enforces them outside the agent loop still a Lab follow-up, not live (#run-limits); the retry ceiling (transient failures ≤2, schema repair once, three failed correction rounds, then escalate), with unknown outcomes parked rather than auto-retried (#retry-ceiling); RED actions, among them send or publish, spend, merge, delete non-junk, permissions and production, always asked of Haiyuan (#gyr-authority), and an approval re-checked against the approved item and current authority right before the action runs (#approval-recheck); a pre-tool gate in our decision layer that, before a high-risk tool-server or shell mutation, returns allow, ask or deny and scores destructive, exfiltration and cost risk (playbook §13, gates table); untrusted content treated as data, never instructions, as policy text that nothing enforces (#untrusted-content); one receipt line per routine run (time, routine, outcome, note), written even when nothing happened (#receipt-line), and weekly receipts, because a bot can summarize its history but should not be its only judge (#kill-review); and, in the controls inventory, the run-limit and fix-round, approval, no-secrets and untrusted-content rows all marked manual, with fix rounds counted by hand, no enforcing wrapper live and no secret scan in the note tool (#controls-inventory). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): an offline trial that evaluates its CPU-only finite-trace rules (BoundedCount, Precedence) on recorded tool trajectories and verifies the HMAC-signed Merkle ledger; then finite-trace checks prototyped on our EM loop's transitions, with session certificates verified offline; and the pack's playbook line: certify sequences, not just individual calls: use lightweight finite-trace temporal logic to catch multi-step attacks that memoryless filters miss, and sign the audit ledger for offline verification. The pack's stop condition: an evaluation step exceeds 1 ms or requires neural-network dependencies. Putting it in front of live tool calls, letting any of its verdicts block a step, or holding the signing key its ledger needs (keys never go in the vault or hub HTML, #extend) would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. Caveats: the attack success rates, false-positive rates, F1 figures, timings and test count are the author's, read in the README, not re-run, and none is ours; its cross-provider normalization has not been tried on our seats' tool calls; the pack's spawn-ok probe shows python3 runs on this Mac, but its version was not checked against 3.9; MIT, 0 stars, created 2026-10-18, pushed 2026-10-21; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: deadweight: static audit of the config an agent silently ignores, with a count ratchet
entries.why: Deterministic static auditor for coding-agent configuration (Python 3.9 or newer, no dependencies, no network; CI on Linux, macOS and Windows) that opens on the failure it targets: 'Your coding agent ignores part of its configuration, and it doesn't tell you.' Two of the real findings in its README: an agent definition missing its name is dropped at load, and calling it gives 'Agent type not found' and nothing else; and a deny rule Bash(git:* push --force) matches nothing, because :* is recognised only at the end of a pattern, so the colon is literal. Its check families: permission rules that never apply and settings in the wrong file; agents and skills that never load, and hooks that never fire (unknown events, matchers that match nothing, scripts that are gone); dead links, rule globs that match no file and dead path anchors; text loaded on every turn that nothing uses (the standing instruction file's size, the always-loaded and skill-listing budgets); skills whose descriptions are close enough to steal each other's triggers; eval suites that cannot fail or cannot run; credentials in files every clone receives; and instruction files placed where their tool does not look. The part the pack would take is the ratchet: --set-floor freezes today's counts and --check-floor fails if they rose, and the floor records the auditor's fingerprint and refuses to compare counts taken by a different auditor version, because 'A measurement with no floor is one people learn to ignore: the numbers move, nobody owns the direction, and a year later every step looked reasonable.' Notices are never omitted, since '0 errors, 0 warnings' is not the whole answer while notices exist, and exemptions cannot silence the checks that audit the overlay or the ratchet itself. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, it is the missing read-side check on the surface our fleet installer writes: the shared skill copies carry no manifest and no checksum, and today's own failure is an instance, one seat's copy of the Lab source-collect skill being malformed, with no YAML frontmatter, so that seat cannot load it by name while the prompt path still works: a skill that never loads, and nothing warns. Per the pack, kept agent-docs-lint (2026-10-11) checks dead references in docs and kept catstack checks symlink and prune install integrity, but neither checks whether a hook fires, whether a skill loads or whether a permission rule can ever match. We already have: a fleet installer that wires the vault's standing instruction files into the homes of the coding CLIs, and the shared skill bundles, canonical in the vault, into the skill homes of two seats and the project mirrors (#skills); in the controls inventory, that wiring marked enforced on the evidence of seven links that resolve to the fleet contract in the vault and one copy whose checksum matches, a check run on demand, not on a schedule (#controls-inventory); a byte ceiling on the two files every agent reads before every task, 13,489 B for the fleet contract and 81,155 B for the never-again list, both sizes recorded in the daily digest (#resident-budget); cited vault paths that must resolve, the Monday card sync checking those cited in the fleet contract and the role cards, with the lint tool not installed (#pointer-check); a new check counted only once it has been seen failing on a deliberately broken input (#check-can-fail); and a Monday kill review that asks of each routine whether it ran, whether its output was right and whether anyone would miss it (#kill-review). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): its read-only audit on a copy of the vault and one project skill mirror, today's counts frozen with --set-floor and --check-floor run in the weekly kill review, a weekly check first and its plugin only if the static pass finds real load failures; and the pack's playbook line: audit what the agent ignores: a permission rule that never matches, a skill that never loads and a hook that never fires are invisible failures; freeze today's count and fail the week if it rises. The pack's stop condition: if the static pass cannot see the skill homes of the two seats it was not built for and finds nothing actionable in the mirrors, keep only the check taxonomy and the ratchet. Running it on the live vault or in a live seat's home, installing its plugin, adding the floor check to the kill review, or taking up its hooks-that-never-fire family, which comes close to the declared-versus-effective hook loading the playbook lists as not adopted (#resident-budget), would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. Caveats: the findings and check families are the author's, read in the README, and none was run on our files; it is shaped for three coding tools, among them the coding-agent harness one of our seats runs, and not for two of our other seats, so it will not see their skill homes unless pointed at them; its opt-in semantic layer sends configuration to a model; its measure flag opens a session of that harness without the workspace-trust dialog, running the project's hooks and tool servers, and the pack puts that flag out of bounds; MIT, 2 stars, created 2026-09-22, pushed 2026-10-22 21:01 PT; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: tripwires: each guard rule carries its incident, its test and a weekly verdict
entries.why: Pre-tool-use guardrail (Node 18.17 or newer, no dependencies, ships CI; hooks for two coding CLIs plus a generic stdin and stdout protocol) that attaches four things to every rule: 'the incident that caused it, the fix the agent should use instead, a test built from the real command, and a weekly report that tells you whether the rule is helping or hurting.' The denial teaches the fix: tripwires try "pkill -f node" prints DENY, the rule id, why the command is wrong ('killing by image name hits every process with that name, including the shell this session runs in'), the exact alternative (list, pick a PID, kill that PID) and the override syntax, and 'The agent reads that text instead of running the command.' The author lists eleven rules, each born from a dated incident with a count of how often it happened first, among them kill-by-name (three times in a month), secret-file-read (six times in five weeks) and deploy-burst (419 deploys and 6,285 credits in a month). Overrides are loud: TRIPWIRES_ALLOW=<rule-id> counts only at the head of a command, and tripwires allow <id> --because "<the person's own words>" takes a one-shot pass and writes those words into the log; in the README's words, 'Nothing stops an agent from typing a reason itself; what this gives you is that every pass is in the report with its justification.' The weekly report gives each rule its denied, overridden, error and session counts and p50 latency, one example line per day and a blank verdict to fill in (helped, hurt, no effect or confounded, with evidence); a hurt verdict backed by three wrong denials means narrowing the rule and adding the real command to its tests. Its parsing rule is 'Data is not code': a heredoc written to a file is not a command, echoing a test runner's name is not an invocation and a trailing comment is not an override; and since rules are code, a rules file cloned in a repo needs an explicit trust step first. It fails open when its engine throws, because a broken guard must not kill the session. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, our never-again list and our hook rules are conclusions without their tests, and the Monday kill review gives no rule a verdict; this supplies the missing lifecycle: date, incident and count, the real denied command as the test, the legitimate neighbours as pass cases, and a weekly helped, hurt or no-effect verdict with evidence. It also forces an explicit fail-open or fail-closed choice, which, per the pack, our fleet has never written down per hook; and per the pack, kept everyhook (2026-10-19) translates one hook source across agents and kept rollcage-guard and bouncer supply the guard mechanism, while this is rule governance, each rule's maintenance record. We already have: the repeat-lesson rule, under which a correction already filed twice or more becomes a proposed fix where the rule is applied, such as a checker or hook spec, after the never-again list came to hold 18 near-identical paragraphs (#repeat-lesson); a byte ceiling on that list (81,155 B), past which a new line means compressing or demoting another (#resident-budget); wrong or outdated lessons put on a prune list and deleted only item by item once Haiyuan approves (#memory-loop); a new check counted only once it has been seen failing on a deliberately broken input (#check-can-fail); the completion-claim rule, prose with no hook installed, any hook for it a separate blind-reviewed trial in audit mode first (#claim-vs-record); a pre-tool gate in our decision layer that returns allow, ask or deny before a high-risk tool-server or shell mutation, a verdict below its confidence floor going to the chief-of-staff route (playbook §13, gates table); and the Monday kill review, which judges each routine, not each rule, against the kill condition its prompt states before it runs (#kill-review, #kill-condition). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the four-field rule record and the weekly report, for never-again entries and for the two or three hook rules that, per the pack, actually deny; a trial of the tool on one seat's coding CLI only, installed with its dry-run flag, with no rule that denies reads except of credential files; and the pack's playbook line: every rule carries its incident, its test, and a weekly verdict: the denial must teach the fix, and a rule nobody has judged in a month is a rule to retire. The pack's stop condition: any rule that denies a read, other than of a credential file, or adds more than 600 ms to a normal call is not adopted. Installing it on a live seat, letting any of its rules deny a call, or setting a hook to fail open or closed would each be a separate Haiyuan decision, and any hook change is Tier 3 under the review-depth rule (#review-depth-tiers). Caveats: the eleven incidents and their counts are the author's, and so is the 200–600 ms start-up cost per matched tool call, measured on a loaded Windows laptop, not on our Mac; it hooks only two coding CLIs, both run by our seats (#roster); its rules are executable code and need a trust step; failing open suits an interactive seat but is the wrong default for CI unless flipped; MIT, 0 stars, created 2026-10-21, pushed 2026-10-22; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: agent-memory: warn-only linter for memory rot, from oversized handoffs to stale facts
entries.why: Plain-file, per-project memory for coding agents (bash plus jq, on macOS and Linux; a session-start hook and a linter) that the author uses daily across about 30 projects, built around a linter for rot. The author's failure list is the useful part: append-only growth (one handoff reached 56 KB with 35 dated sections, and one index had 31 current-state bullets, injected into every session); stale state, such as being logged out of a site or waiting on something, read as current by the next agent; the same rule in four places, drifted apart; no mechanical check, so everything depended on agents behaving; a hook that forced writes, later removed: 'A Stop hook blocked the agent whenever files changed but memory didn't. Agents complied by appending something every turn.'; and two parallel memories that can contradict each other. Its linter, memory-check, warns and never blocks, on: a handoff over 6 KB, older than 7 days or with 3 or more dated headings (the append-only smell); a waiting or running section 2 or more days old; an index over 8 KB or with more than 3 current-state bullets; index links that point nowhere, and records the index does not list; records without a status, or with a superseded-by pointer to a missing file; and facts stamped as of a date older than 3 days. Limits are environment variables, and the warnings surface at session start beside the index and the handoff, with the handoff's age. Its design rules are the transferable part: the handoff is a snapshot, not a log, rewritten whole while git keeps history; one home per fact, standing rules in the agent's standing instruction file and project knowledge in memory; volatile state kept out or date-stamped for the linter; decisions superseded, not deleted; 'check mechanically, nudge softly'; and no forced writes, since staleness is caught at the next session start instead of by making every turn write something. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, the vault is our durable memory, and its handoffs and packs are append-only artifacts: every day adds a pack, the shared Today note grows, and a waiting-on line sits in notes long after the wait ended. Per the pack, kept Agentic Vault Skeleton (2026-10-14) covers layout, kept vault-memory (2026-10-20) covers recall and the kept memory-loop card covers write discipline, but none has numeric rot thresholds or a 'snapshot, not log' rule; and the negative result is as valuable as the linter: a stop hook that forces a memory write every turn teaches agents to append noise, a direct warning for any rule to write a learning note after every task that we are tempted to tighten. We already have: the vault as the team's long-term memory, a context repo rather than a chat log, whose daily consolidation merges lessons that say the same thing (#vault); the memory loop: write only what is new, open every note with a one-line summary that recall greps, keep the post-task note mandatory, keep Decision notes as the audit trail with a superseded one pointed to by its replacement, and delete durable lessons only after Haiyuan approves each item, policy text that nothing enforces (#memory-loop); fast-clock facts (Mac connected, a PR tip, quota, CI state) re-fetched live before any action or claim rather than remembered, and a provenance card (claim, source, owner, status, supersedes, review_after) on each new Decision note and standing-rule memory (#memory-rules); for shared user memory, one dated, sourced line per fact, a replaced fact forgotten in the same turn (an exception to the rule that deleting non-junk needs Haiyuan, but only in the drafter's reading, which Haiyuan has not yet ruled on; every other forget waits for Haiyuan's approval) and a Monday prune pass that only proposes (#shared-memory-admission); a byte ceiling on the two files every agent reads before every task, 13,489 B for the fleet contract and 81,155 B for the never-again list, both sizes recorded in the daily digest (#resident-budget); and cited vault paths that must resolve, the Monday card sync checking those in the fleet contract and the role cards, with the lint tool not installed (#pointer-check). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): only its linter, about one shell script, ported onto a copy of the vault with the 6 KB, 7-day and 3-heading defaults and kept warn-only for two weeks before any hook blocks, measuring how many handoffs trip; not its stop hook, and not its installer's import into the live global configuration; and the pack's playbook line: lint the memory, not just the code: cap the handoff and index by size and age, rewrite the handoff as a snapshot, and never force a write every turn. The pack's stop condition: if it fires on most packs and nobody reads the warnings, retire it, and add no blocking hook. Running it on the live vault, scheduling it, adding any hook, or rewriting notes as snapshots, while our deletes of durable lessons stay item by item with Haiyuan's approval (#memory-loop), would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. Caveats: the failure list and the thresholds are the author's, from the author's own projects, not tuned on our vault; its installer edits the global standing instruction files of two coding CLIs between markers, a live-config write that must not run unattended; warnings never block, so it works only if someone reads them at session start; MIT, 0 stars, created and pushed 2026-10-21 20:21 PT; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.

entries.title: mac-dev-janitor: kills a runaway process group, then leaves the agent a note why
entries.why: Two parts for a Mac that runs many coding agents (Python for the watchdog, shell for the cleanup, two launchd agents, no sudo). Its resource watchdog samples ps every 10 s and groups processes by process group, since 'Coding agents run each shell command in its own group, so one group is one command.'; it sends SIGTERM, then SIGKILL 10 s later, to a group with a physical footprint of 8 GB or more (or the largest group, at 1.5 GB or more, after 30 s of memory pressure), a group that used 3 or more cores while the machine was at least 85% busy for 2 minutes, a group that used 0.9 cores or more for 20 minutes straight, or an orphaned dev tool older than 3 hours (its parent died, no terminal). Eligibility is narrow: only descendants of a list of known coding agents, or a known dev tool started from a terminal or orphaned; never touched are any group containing an agent or a terminal emulator, app bundles (editors and their language servers), system binaries and launchd jobs, and shells, so the shell returns exit 143 to the agent instead of vanishing. The note is the mechanism: every kill is logged as JSON lines, notified and printed to the process's terminal, and an overload, runaway or memory kill is also appended to a kills file in the user's state folder, with the command's working directory and an instruction for the agent; a bundled agent-rules file tells the agent to read that file and run a smaller command instead of retrying the same one, and the installer can append it to the agent's standing instruction file. A daily cleanup runs at 20:00 through a launchd agent: git worktree remove, never forced, for one tool's settled or orphaned worktrees, a purge of node_modules, dist and target folders in projects untouched for 7 days, a cache clean, a container prune and deletion of unavailable simulators, with a dry-run flag to preview it. Why it matters here: per the collection pack, it aims at host survival rather than agent logic, while our watchdogs judge the run log, not the machine; two rules transfer: kill the process group, not the process, since a test runner's workers hide behind an idle root; and 'a kill without a note is a retry', since an agent that sees only exit 143 runs the same command again, so the kills file plus the agent rule is what breaks the loop. Per the pack, kept whystuck and watchdog-kit watch the agent's progress, while this watches the host's memory, load and orphan set, and it gives the 15 GB floor a concrete pre-launch cleanup path with a dry run. We already have: long launches held while the Mac has less than 15 GB free, a floor since 2026-10-11 (#launch) that only one queue's disk gate enforces, the shared launcher having no disk check (#controls-inventory); the Mac run lessons: launches held at 12–14 GB until space was freed, a nearly full disk the likely cause of an app-level disconnect on 10-11, and the 10-15 exec wedge, in which newly started programs hung before running (#mac-run-lessons); after any Mac trouble, two timed spawn-ok probes that must exit 0 before any launch, relaunch or resume (#spawn-ok); a stale-log watchdog (~540 s) on every long run, whose on-stale action resumes the same session (#launch), and, since 2026-10-20 12:16 PT, an ownership guard that refuses a restart unless the old process is proven dead, since killing a stale tmux session does not prove the old agent stopped (#watchdog-resume-safety); named long-CLI failure modes (crash, hang, stall, api-error), each to leave a machine-readable heartbeat saying whether the run finished and what killed it (#exception-first); unknown outcomes after a crash or dirty exit parked, not auto-retried (#retry-ceiling); Mac checks that only report, never kill, installed with no schedule (#report-only-checks); and deleting non-junk on the RED list, always asked of Haiyuan (#gyr-authority). What would be adopted, per the collection pack's recommendation (a proposal, not approved): the watchdog in dry-run mode for one week on this Mac, then only its memory and runaway rules, at a 12 GB group threshold and a 20-minute runaway window; its cleanup's dry run ported as the pre-launch disk check, with the container prune left off; and the pack's playbook line: kill the process group, and leave the agent a note: an idle root hides its workers; exit 143 without a reason is just a retry. The pack's kill condition: any kill of an agent or terminal group, any container volume prune, or a false kill on a legitimate long build kills the trial. Letting it kill anything on this Mac, scheduling either part, appending its rule to a seat's standing instruction file, or any delete beyond a dry run would each be a separate Haiyuan decision. Caveats: it was created on the day of the pack, and its README states no test suite, so per the pack it is a well-described script, not a proven tool; its container cleanup (a system prune and a volume prune, both with the all flag) deletes every unused volume, a data risk the pack says not to enable; its purge deletes dependency folders in repos untouched for 7 days, rebuildable but slow to recover; cleanup needs Full Disk Access for a wrapper app; its thresholds are the author's defaults, and the pack calls the 8 GB default high for a 24 GB machine already near the free-space floor, yet its trial uses a 12 GB group threshold; MIT, 0 stars, created and pushed 2026-10-22; README-verified only, not installed or run. Reference only; any workflow change, live-seat install, hook or settings change needs Haiyuan. No new seat. Lab card; appliedToPlaybook false.
